title: 'All we did was fun stuff': ACT public school system in 'crisis'
text:
Primary school students Thea and Elvy Bundey said they have spent much of their week colouring in instead of learning.

Due to staff shortages, their classes have been combined, resulting in 63 students being in one class.

"All we did was fun stuff and I would prefer to learn and do fun stuff than just do fun stuff," Year 1 student Thea said.

It is a common story across public schools in the ACT, and is one of the reasons why teachers and school staff have again taken industrial action amid protracted negotiations on a new enterprise agreement.

'Teachers are leaving'

Schools across the ACT were closed for two hours on Thursday morning as Australian Education Union (AEU) members stopped work to letterbox communities about the situation.

"Frustration levels are pretty high," Dickson College teacher Tom Griffith said.

"Public schools are under-resourced, teachers are leaving, or we are not able to get new teachers in the profession at the rate we need them."

Dickson College teacher Tom Griffith was among peers who took industrial action on Thursday. (ABC News: Monte Bovill)

It is the third time schools have closed this year due to industrial action, with the first being a two-hour work stoppage in May, followed by a full-day strike in June.

There was also minimal supervision for students for two hours last week, as union members met to consider the government's latest offer.

Freya Bundey, who is also a teacher at Dickson College, said the public school system was in "crisis".

"My classes, for most of the year, have been over capacity," she said.

" If we have got less funding for students … we are going to keep haemorrhaging kids to the private sector. "

Dickson College teacher Freya Bundey spent the morning letterboxing Canberra residents. (ABC News: Monte Bovill)

Conversations about workloads

The union's ACT branch president Angela Burroughs said the public education system was "suffering from chronic understaffing".

"We have reports from our members saying that they are supervising up to 90 students at one time — that is a system that is under immense strain," she said.

She flagged the potential for more industrial action later in the year, including another full-day strike, if the ACT government did not improve its offer.

Education Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith said negotiations had made some progress, particularly on pay, but said there was still work to be done.

"The conversation now is about workload, it's about classroom management, it's about those split and collapsed classes, how we get better visibility of that and how we centrally better support schools to manage those teacher absences," she said.

Some schools to get less funding

While enterprise negotiations have been ongoing, there has been concern about individual school budgets and staffing levels for 2027.

A new funding model, taking effect next year, aims to address overspending and redistribute existing resources according to students' needs.

Some schools are facing a drop in their funding, but Ms Stephen-Smith said only indicative budgets have been released so far, with final allocations still to come.

"These are definitely challenging conversations, and for some schools it will be a reduction in their budget from 2026 to 2027," she said.

" It is important we get back to a fair, equitable and sustainable funding model. "

Education Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith says some schools will get less funding but budget decisions are yet to be finalised. (ABC News: Monte Bovill)

Ms Stephen-Smith said an "exceptions bucket" of money would be made available to schools that struggled to meet the conditions of the new funding model.

"Every school is different, every school is facing different opportunities and different challenges," she said.

She also said she was concerned that support staff at some of Canberra's public schools had been told they might not have a job before budget decisions had been finalised.

"I was really distressed to hear that feedback about learning support assistants being given that advice at this point," she said.

"These are indicative budgets, and this is an ongoing conversation. There will be some changes that need to be made."

title: Another setback for beleaguered Cape du Couedic wave buoy
text:
South Australian fishers and surfers will have to wait about another month before its beleaguered Bureau of Meteorology (BOM) wave buoy is redeployed off Kangaroo Island.

Despite BOM planning to reinstate the Cape du Couedic wave buoy last week after a "lightning strike" nearly four months ago put it out of commission, a new complication has caused further delays.

"Final pre-deployment checks identified an issue with the buoy's satellite communications, so deployment has been postponed while the issue is fixed," a BOM spokesperson said.

" To ensure reliability and longevity of the replacement buoy, the bureau has opted to install a new mooring as part of the redeployment rather than reuse the existing one. "

BOM wave buoy redeployment The Bureau of Meteorology wave buoy has only been operational for about 10 months in two years, but replacement parts have been secured following its most outage and it's expected to be transmitting data again this week.

A failure of the buoy's mooring system caused it to break free and wash up on Kangaroo Island in November 2025, putting it out of commission for six weeks.

That failure had followed a long, nine-month delay to repair the buoy from September 2024, after it started transmitting erroneous data and was recalled.

BOM blamed the delay on a supply issue to source a "specialist mooring" from Canada.

As a consequence, the buoy has only been operational for about 10 months in two years, and its ongoing issues are frustrating communities.

"We understand the value of the Cape du Couedic wave buoy observations to the coastal community," the BOM spokesperson said.

"The bureau is expecting new mooring components to arrive shortly and anticipates the wave buoy will be operational again by late October 2026.

"The timing for safe deployment is also dependent on favourable weather conditions."

Federal Environment Minister Murray Watt last week said an independent review into BOM was currently underway and was providing the opportunity "to look at tools and services, and how BOM can continue to improve its service offering to Australians into the future".

A spotter buoy deployed by Flinders University researchers at Victor Harbor in early 2025. (Website: Flinders University)

The Cape de Couedic wave buoy is SA's only BOM-operated wave buoy.

When functioning, it issues real-time and historical data about significant and maximum wave heights, average and peak wave period, and swell direction.

Its data is used by commercial and recreational fishers, surfers and the likes of abalone divers, who use swell period data to gauge water visibility.

The lack of data on BOM's wave buoy webpage is a familiar sight for South Australians.

While BOM was "working to restore bureau observations", the spokesperson advised communities to view data from several spotter buoys launched along SA's coastline by Flinders University researchers this decade.

Supported by two coastal councils and running in conjunction with the South Australian Research and Development Institute, SA Water, the Environment Protection Authority, the SA Department for Environment and Water, and the Integrated Marine Observing System, the project seeks to better inform coastal management and sand drift, and mitigate erosion.

title: More Tasmanian campsites to require bookings to address 'ghost camping'
text:
Campers will be able to book a site at some of Tasmania's most popular campgrounds from early November, under the first phase of a new online booking system for national parks.

"Only those campgrounds that currently attract a fee to stay are included in the first phase of the system," Parks Minister Nick Duigan said.

Campgrounds at 10 places managed by the Parks and Wildlife Service (PWS) are included in the first phase:

Arthur Pieman Conservation Area

Peggs Beach Conservation Area

Narawntapu National Park

Mount William National Park

Maria Island National Park

Freycinet National Park

Fortescue Bay, Tasman National Park

South Bruny National Park

Mount Field National Park

PWS project manager Chris Evans said the new system would address "ghost camping" — where campers reserve sites with an unoccupied tent or van until they are ready to use the site.

Tasmania looks to halt 'ghost camping' "Ghost camping" is again a hot topic as frustrated holiday-makers find empty tents or caravans reserving sites at campgrounds.

"You've got to go in, make a reservation [and] pay for your reservation at that time," Mr Evans said.

"If you come up to the date that you're due to arrive and then cancel it at that point, you will lose your full fee."

Mr Duigan said he wanted campers to have certainty.

"If you book your site, pay for your site there is every expectation that when you turn up to that site, your site is there and ready for you," he said.

" If someone has put their tent down on it but haven't paid for it and haven't booked it, then there is a reasonable expectation that they will be moved off and you will be moved in. "

Mount Field National Park is one of the places included in the first phase of the booking system. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

Mr Duigan said all of the sites subject to the booking system were places where PWS staff were on the ground and ready to help educate campers.

"We'll be taking a pretty soft-touch approach to that in the early days."

He said further phases of the system would be worked through.

Asked whether free campsites would require bookings in later iterations of the system, Mr Duigan said:

"I would like to see a circumstance where all of the Parks [and Wildlife Service] offerings are included through this interface because that gives people the certainty we want to provide."

Other PWS offerings will be added to the system.

"Once fully implemented, the system will enable customers to book campsites, walking experiences, cave tours, parks passes and other products through a single online portal," Mr Duigan said.

Nick Duigan says he wants campers to have certainty. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Visit Northern Tasmania chief executive Tracey Mallett said the tourism industry was "looking forward" to the implementation of the booking system.

"It does bring us in line with the rest of the country and [it's] perfect timing of course with the introduction of the new Spirits of Tasmania because those new ships, which obviously launch at the end of October, will bring two and a half times more caravanners over the course of a week," Ms Mallett said.

"Being able to book ahead guarantees that they will get that site."

title: Coal mine owners walk away and leave rehabilitation to state
text:
A central Queensland mine has been abandoned and will now be managed by the state government.

Owners of the Bluff coal mine, Bowen Coking Coal (BCC), went into voluntary administration in July last year, with McGrathNicol's Mark Holland and Shaun Fraser appointed as administrators.

The open cut mine is south of the township of Bluff, located 20 kilometres east of Blackwater and 174km west of Rockhampton.

The Department of Natural Resources and Mines confirmed the liquidators had "disclaimed" the mining lease, associated environmental authority and exploration permits for the mine.

"This means the mining lease has ceased, the site is now an abandoned mine and will be managed by the Queensland government," a department spokesperson said.

" The department has secured the site and is working with relevant agencies to ensure risks to public safety and the environment are appropriately managed. "

Bowen Coking Coal purchased the Bluff coal mine from Carabella Resources in 2021.

Carabella Resources was granted the original 15-year mining lease over the site by the state government in 2016, for up to 1.8 million tonnes per annum of metallurgical coal.

It began mining on the site in 2019.

The following year, coal prices fell and Carabella Resources went into voluntary administration in November 2020. At the time, the coal price was $US72 per tonne.

The mine was placed into care and maintenance in December 2020, before Bowen Coking Coal restarted operations, and it mined its first coal in the first quarter of 2022.

Bowen Coking Coal shipped its first trains of coal in June 2022 and at the time planned to mine 5 million tonnes of product across all of its operations by 2024. (ABC News: Nathan Morris)

At the time, the managing director said the company was planning on mining 5 million tonnes of product across all its operations by 2024.

On September 14 this year, a notice was published on the Australian Securities and Investments Commission website to formally wind up the overarching Bowen PCI Pty Ltd company.

State takes on rehabilitation works

Rehabilitation works at the Bluff coal mine site will now be managed through the department's Abandoned Mine Lands Program.

Lock the Gate's Central Queensland coordinator Claire Gronow said this created a number of concerns.

"This is kind of uncharted territories. Although there's heaps of abandoned coal mines around Queensland, including the notorious Mount Morgan gold mine, that the government is required to manage, this is a relatively recent occurrence for a coal mine to simply walk away," Dr Gronow said.

Most mines are moved over to the program after they reach their end of life and have rehabilitation works done. In the case of the Bluff coal mine, it was still an active mine site when it closed.

"Obviously, the mine didn't go its full life," Dr Gronow said.

"The rehabilitation plans would probably need to be redrawn to deal with the fact that they're halfway through the mine."

The Queensland government will now manage and rehabilitate the Bluff coal mine. (Supplied: Department of Natural Resources and Mines)

Money for the rehabilitation works comes out of the state government's financial provisioning scheme, which is also currently under review.

"The Queensland government holds a certain amount of money in a kind of a trust to cover these situations and that's contributed to by the mining companies," Dr Gronow said.

The department or the Queensland Treasury were unable to disclose what funds were paid to the state for the rehabilitation.

The environmental permit for the Bluff coal mine, published on the Queensland government's website, shows an estimated rehabilitation cost of $12,251,470.50, as of November 6 last year,

"That seems a little low possibly, particularly since it hasn't been actively managed for the last year or two," Dr Gronow said.

She said there appeared to have been some earthworks done but aerial footage showed a large hole in the ground and ponds of water.

The site also needed ongoing environmental management, Dr Gronow said.

"Even when it's not operating, it's a source of dust, every time the wind blows, particularly in the dry weather that we've been having, there's a dust cloud," she said.

"One of the requirements is that they're supposed to have someone on standby who can get to the site immediately in the case of rainfall, for pumps and things like that to manage the water and stop unauthorised overflows of water.

"We don't know who's doing that now, we don't know who's covering the cost, we don't know who's going to cover the cost of dust management on the site and it's quite difficult with around 500 hectares of bare land just sitting there."

title: Farmers cut deal with government over backpacker visa delays
text:
The National Farmers Federation (NFF) has cut a deal with the federal government for faster processing of backpacker visas.

Limits to backpacker numbers, announced by Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke last week, sparked worker shortage fears in regional areas.

A slowdown on visa processing began in August, leaving a gaping hole in the harvest workforce and working holiday-makers in limbo.

NFF chief executive Michael Guerin said farmers have had a reprieve.

"(The government has) reacted quickly on what is a critical and urgent need," he said.

"We've put together what's described as a good faith deal where none of the usual checks and balances are in place," he said.

Michael Guerin says farmers have reached a 'good faith' deal with the government. (Supplied: National Farmers Federation)

Urgent visas to be processed 'instantly'

Mr Guerin said the deal will hopefully unblock some of the critical labour shortage problems.

"[The] government are relying on us to put forward only the most urgent visa applications in the system that need to be processed now, and they'll accept those in good faith and prioritise that processing," he said.

"In the last 24 hours, we've been able to go from a standing start to a system which is in place today."

Working holiday-makers are essential for fruit picking and harvesting. (Supplied: Alice Rye)

The NFF expects the agreement will allow for some applications to be processed in a matter of days.

"We don't know exactly the numbers we'll be putting through to Home Affairs each day. They don't know the numbers they'll be receiving," Mr Guerin said.

"But again, the spirit of this is that in good faith, we will put forward the most judicial ones and in good faith they will try and process those pretty much instantaneously."

Silage contractors have faced worker shortages because of the visa slowdown. (ABC News: Emily Bissland)

Mr Guerin said it had been a difficult time for farmers.

"The facts are that Australian agriculture relies completely on these working holiday-maker visas, on overseas labour in various forms."

"Communities are suffering, producers are suffering, we're unable to get crops off," he said.

While the NFF has welcomed the government's fast-tracked approvals, Mr Guerin is concerned it does not deal with the issue in the long run.

"Regional communities more generally rely on these overseas workers doing roles that we can't find Australians to do," he said.

"That will be the case going forward."

"[This] doesn't provide any long-term solutions and the broader reform of migration."

Farmers haven't had enough workers for the busy harvest time. (Supplied)

State farming organisations and commodity groups will help organise the most urgent applications.

Workers need to have already applied for a Working Holiday Maker visa to be considered.

They also need to engage in agricultural work on a specific farm and their labour and timely arrival need to be critical to business operations.

Submissions through the new process do not guarantee expedited processing or visa approval either, as applications remain subject to Department of Home Affairs assessment processes.

A department spokesperson said the government recognised the contribution of Working Holiday Makers (WHMs) to the economy and the labour market.

"There are a small group of WHMs who head straight to the regions and use their particular skills to support our agriculture sector," they said.

"The Department will work with the National Farmers Federation on identifying and prioritising people with specific skills in the agricultural sector who have applied for a WHM visa, have contracted with an employer to provide their skills to undertake agricultural work and need to be here inside 3 months," they said.

title: Outback date farm bounces back after crop destroyed by rain
text:
The Northern Territory's largest date farm is on the road to recovery after heavy rains in February seriously damaged the operation, with early signs pointing to a solid crop developing in the coming months.

Large parts of Central Australia and the Barkly region were impacted by severe weather and flooding earlier this year, as the entire Northern Territory experienced a significant wet season.

The 2026 harvest was destroyed by major rains across Central Australia in February. (Supplied: Kim McKay)

The rain came at a terrible time for the Tamara Date Plantation, 70 kilometres south-east of Alice Springs, with the downpour starting at the same time as the harvest and destroying much of the crop.

However, the Desert Fruit Company, the cooperative that owns the date farm, is focusing on coming back stronger, and workers are in the field pollinating the palms in preparation for harvest early next year.

Pollinating process

Like many commercial date farms, the palm trees at the Tamara Date Plantation are manually pollinated.

Workers remove the pollen from the male plant, place it in a jar connected to two pipes, and blow it onto the female plant when it opens its spathe.

Kim McKay removes pollen from a male plant, which will be used to manually pollinate the farm's date palms. (ABC Rural: Charles Geary)

This process started in June, which was ahead of schedule as some of the trees had flowered earlier than usual.

The next stage in the process is bagging, which company director and farmer Kim McKay said would be in full swing by October, with many palms requiring bagging at the same time.

"You're trying to bag as many as you can each day, mainly to protect them from birds and to a lesser extent certain insects," Mr McKay said.

Signs of a good season

With an earlier start to pollination, some palms could be ready for harvest soon, but most of it will come towards the end of February and the start of March.

Some of the few remaining dates from the 2025 harvest at the Tamara Date Plantation. (ABC Rural: Charles Geary)

Mr McKay said the plantation usually fluctuated between stronger and weaker seasons on a yearly basis, due to variation in the flowering process, but this should be a good year.

"Our plantation has a biennial nature to it, whereas one year we get a real lot of flowers and then the next year not quite as many," he said.

" And this year we would normally expect to have a lot of flowers and that is indeed happening. "

Ramadan changes business plan

The largest market for the farm's Barhi dates has been Muslim communities observing Ramadan, as the Islamic holy period coincided with the harvest period in recent years.

However, Ramadan is moving further away from the harvest, as it follows the lunar cycle and occurs approximately 10 days earlier each year in the Gregorian calendar.

The date farm is 70km south-east of Alice Springs, with harvest expected to begin in late February to March. (ABC Rural: Charles Geary)

The fruit would be transported during its yellow, or khalal, stage to ensure it was ready for Ramadan, which required cool storage to prevent further ripening.

As the timing of this became more challenging, Mr McKay said the farm had decided to look into other market opportunities.

"As [Ramadan] moves away from our harvest time, we decided we don't want to take the risk any longer of providing a date that is fraught with difficulty keeping in the hard, yellow sage," Mr McKay said.

title: How 'Auskick for oldies' is saving lives in country Victoria
text:
David O'Brien is in the "echo" of his football career.

The 55-year-old reckons he's played about 860 games in his lifetime, and for the past seven years, all those games have all been in Masters football leagues, competitions strictly for over 35s.

In Country Masters footy they don't keep official scores. Kicking goals are beside the point.

It might be a bit slower, sloppier and less serious than the younger men's competitions, but as long as you're playing, you're a winner.

"I call it Footy Valhalla," O'Brien says, sitting in a shed of his Great Ocean Road farm, a bit more than an hour before he heads to Torquay for game number 861-or-so.

David O'Brien knocking out a few last minute jobs before swapping the farm for footy (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

"So, your real footy career was your proper footy career where you're playing for points and where it matters. Don't try and translate that 'rah-rah', high testosterone energy into Masters, it's not really what it's all about.

" It's an echo of your footy career. What it's designed to do is capture all that off-field stuff — all that mateship, camaraderie, men's mental health. "

David is a Masters football evangelist — singing the praises of the over-35s game which is booming in country Victoria.

Player numbers in the Victorian Country AFL Masters competition have almost doubled over the past five years, with 819 players now registered across 16 teams. They're all men's teams for now, but the league hopes to launch a women's competition soon.

While the health benefits of staying active while aging are self-evident, the benefit Masters players enjoy comes from simply being involved and is more intangible.

For a demographic most at risk of social isolation and suicide — regional men aged 35-54 — Masters footy may literally be saving lives.

A football is never far away at David O'Brien's farm. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

'Bring your boots'

David O'Brien is one-of-a-kind.

He's a farmer, a barrister, a musician and has a few business ventures including selling alpaca-wool beanies and 'honey-wine' mead. He was also previously a National Party MP and country town hotelier.

David O'Brien catching up with teammates before the bounce (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

He's the kind of guy you might see dressed in a full suit and tie one day, and then blue jeans held up by a hay bale chord the next.

As a devoted amateur footballer, he has also been busy sharing the gospel of Masters footy close to home — helping launch new team the South Coast Sharks in 2023.

David's lacing up his boots for the Sharks today, preparing to ditch the pressures of an eclectic, busy life and spend a few hours focusing on little more than having a kick with mates.

Physio tape is handy for running repairs on both boots and bodies (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

"[As a barrister] I deal with some not pretty things in society, and so seeing just the simplicity of a game of football… it is, I guess, 'me' time, but it's 'us' time for the team," he says.

" I've already got that buzz looking forward to what's going to happen on the ground. "

Before the bounce

Winter is breathing its last gasps in Torquay. It's the last weekend of August, and the final round of the Country Masters season.

The forecast rain hasn't appeared on the coast, so the Ballarat Diggers arrive to a brilliantly sunny afternoon — albeit with just enough players to fill a single team, rather than the double-header originally planned.

It's no problem in Masters football though, where the distance between clubs often means the away teams come up short.

You're never too old for a few lollies to keep the energy up while playing footy (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

The men decide to combine the age groups and play a game of "six quarters", with a few Sharks players happily kitting up for the Diggers to further even out the playing field.

It's an example of the contrast between competitive club footy and Masters, where the focus is on participation over performance, and the motto is 'football for fun'.

That being said, there are some more official differences.

A few minor rule modifications are in place to help avoid injuries and keep the focus on fun. Rough tackles are out, so is raising your knee in marking or ruck contests.

The South Coast Sharks get an address from their coach before the game (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

Games are played fortnightly instead of weekly, giving older bodies a bit of extra time to recover, and most games aren't officially scored.

In the Away Team rooms, the Diggers are stretching and strapping dodgy knees, ankles and shoulders. Black electrical tape is also being wound around players' left arms.

The impermanence of life has been on Ballarat Coach Shane Jewell's mind this week.

His great mate and beloved club stalwart, Frank Cranage, died three days ago following a long-term illness. He was the third Digger to have died of health issues in the last few years.

Standing arm-in-arm with his teammates for his pre-game address, Shane only manages a couple of words before his voice falters, and tears break through.

"Looking at you guys now, we don't know what's going to happen down the track, so you really gotta enjoy everything, okay?" he says.

"'Cos you don't know what's going to happen five or 10 years from now.

" So, this one, play for Frankie… play, have fun. "

Shane Jewell is consoled by teammates after a tearful pre-game address (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

Numbers booming

You're never really alone on a football field.

Shortly after the dressing room tears have been wiped away, Jewell is in a circle of 50-odd men in the middle of the Torquay footy ground, arm-in-arm with both his teammates and the Sharks.

Sharks and Diggers stand together before the bounce (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

Smiles have replaced sorrow by the time today's umpire gives the group a last-minute address.

"We all wanna go to work on Monday, so footy for fun — let's go enjoy ourselves," he says, before the players head to their positions together, already chatting and joking with one another.

The emphasis on mateship had Country Masters Vic President Jason Aspland immediately hooked after joining his local Shepparton Masters club four years ago.

"What I noticed straight away with Masters was the camaraderie," Aspland says. "The group were very much about making sure everybody was having fun."

Victoria Country AFL Masters president Jason Aspland (ABC News: Charmaine Manuel)

"Instead of worrying about winning or losing, we're more worried about participation — making sure everybody's enjoying themselves, making sure everybody gets to work on Monday, nice, safe, and healthy.

" It is a bit of an AusKick for oldies type of a thing. "

The game is booming in country Victoria, with official participation jumping from 441 registered players in 2021 to 819 signed-up this year.

This official increase of 86 per cent in five years is widely considered to be lower than the real numbers — with likely hundreds of unregistered players joining in regular trainings or unofficial social groups attached to the league's 16 clubs.

There's an argument that Masters football may be the fastest growing form of AFL, but Mr Aspland doesn't see any particularly exciting reason behind the increase.

"I think the biggest growth in Masters football across the country — not just Vic Country — is education," he says. "It's learning that Masters football is here, and that there are other options for footballers once they're finished playing Saturday football."

It's a balmy Sunday afternoon, and the Diggers and Sharks are having a blast. Together.

The Sharks are the classier team throughout the first couple of quarters, stretching out a commanding lead in a game where the score will never be officially recorded.

Suicide and social isolation

Opposition is a misnomer in Masters footy.

After scratching their competitive itch for a couple of quarters, the Sharks are winning 71 to 6.

So, they ease off. A few of the handier South Coast players pull on Ballarat jumpers and the game swings into a more evenly matched hit-out.

It might not be the footy of their heyday, but players on both sides execute brilliant passages of play with somewhat unexpected regularity. As the well-worn footy cliche goes, form might be temporary, but class is permanent.

The game rolls on in the afternoon sun, with each goal met with cheers and high fives for the goalkicker, delivered by players from both teams.

It doesn't matter what jumper you're wearing in Masters footy, everyone celebrates together (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

It's this camaraderie which shows just how fortunately positioned Country Masters is to provide an antidote to two key challenges faced by older men in regional Victoria: social isolation and suicide.

Regional and rural Victorians have higher rates of social isolation compared to those in the city, with men aged between 35 and 54 most at risk of suicide.

Sharks coach Luke Vassallo, who helped launch the Sharks with David O'Brien, sees Masters football as an invaluable way of combating loneliness.

South Coast Sharks Coach Luke Vassallo (centre) (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

"I think the hardest pressures in life come through from sort of 30 to 50, you know, bringing up young kids, mortgages, et cetera," he says. "And people keeping their jobs and trying to build a family and build, I guess, a legacy for their own family.

"One of the big things that we've established and witnessed and experienced here at the Sharks is venting with your mates at training, in particular, and at game time, talking about life.

"It's tremendously important to be able to share that and not feel alone."

Jason Aspland sees a clear comparison to one of regional Victoria's most-loved community spaces for older men.

"Masters football in some ways is one of the biggest men's sheds that there is across the country," he says.

"It's a place where those that are mature age can find other like-minded people, they can gather friendship in that way, they can then go out, have a kick of the footy, have some fun, come back at the end and have a chat, tell stories, do all their bits that may not have been able to be possible for those people if they didn't have Master's football."

One of the many volunteers making game days possible, a watchful goal umpire (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

David O'Brien has seen firsthand how the impact of suicides can seep through regional communities. He's also seen the preventative power of social connection.

"It really hurts," he says. "I've had three or four people suicide… it is a terrible thing and it affects those left shockingly for a long period of time.

" We've lost some people… involved in our master's community to male suicide, but I've certainly seen a lot more saved than lost. "

It's all about connection

Matt Jones could be a poster boy for the adage of class being permanent.

'Jonesy' gave footy away when he was 22 and had started working weekends back in Gippsland. Now 49 and living in Anglesea, he's into his second year with the Sharks.

It's rare to see Matt Jones without a grin at the footy (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

Despite the 26-year footy hiatus, he's still got a bag of tricks to go along with his silver-blonde hair and seemingly perpetual grin.

Clean hands, a quick first step and a dead-eye in front of goal, this afternoon he's showing signs of what so many Masters players like to joke about — how good they were 'back in the day'.

But reliving the glory years is not what Matt Jones is getting out of Masters football. It's all about just being involved.

"It's just been awesome. One of the best things I've done," he says, grinning.

"The group of boys that we're playing with, they're just legends. I Just love that part of it. Just, you know, new friendships.

"Socially, like half a dozen or so of the boys, we swim every morning at 7 o'clock, go for an ocean swim… [and] just around the street we're always bumping into each other."

While there's no single, simple solution to social isolation and suicide, the opportunity to connect with community offered by Masters clubs is invaluable.

Founder and coach Luke Vassallo never predicted just how quickly the Sharks would build a close-knit community of its own on the Surf Coast.

"Now we've got something like 130 members," Vassallo says. "So, I've met 130 people I never met in my life, in a reasonably small country town.

"You bump into people at the supermarket and all of those things, which I think is a tremendous thing that we've built."

And much like Masters football throughout the state, the Sharks are still growing.

After the final siren

The simple beauty of Masters footy is easy to see in Torquay, as the sun begins its slow descent towards the horizon.

As the final siren blares, nobody on the field bothers to look at the scoreboard.

Instead, the players shake hands and continue the laughter that has permeated a unique six quarters of football. Then, they walk off the ground together, as one.

After the siren goes, the Sharks and Diggers are one team (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

After hot showers all round, players from both sides join together for the post-game meal typically organised by the home team — which today is paella.

For the final hour or so of the afternoon drinks are shared, awards of the day are announced, old war stories are relived between mates, and a few dozen over-35 men do what they all really came here to do — be a part of a community.

The next day

Footy in country Victoria is a game full of simple life lessons, David O'Brien reckons.

"It's unpredictable," he says, sitting in the shed where he'll soon be shaking off any soreness from yesterday's footy game to get his sheep shorn and crutched.

"There have been some masters — Gary Ablett, Buddy Franklin, people who can just dominate the game — but for the rest of us mere mortals, it's a challenge to try and do the things that you can sometimes do.

" Sometimes the ball sits up for you and other times it doesn't, and I suppose that's a bit of an analogy for life. "

With about 861 games now under his hay bale cord belt, there's still little sign of slowing down. Even despite the knees, which ache more than they used to, the nuisance of a couple of recently broken fingers, and the occasional limp-inducing corkie.

"It is a game I will probably play all my life. I threaten to give up every now and then, but I've been doing that for years. I've retired more times than Johnny Farnham," he says.

"There'll be hopefully another good couple of seasons left, and that's what it's all about."

title: Matildas name three uncapped players in squad for October friendlies
text:
After suffering a gut-wrenching ACL injury on the eve of her potential Matildas debut, midfielder Hana Lowry has been handed a national team recall.

Coach Joe Montemurro has named three uncapped players for his 26-player squad, which will face world number three Germany and world number 47 Haiti in Europe in October.

One of them is Lowry, who was previously selected in 2024 but was ruled out with a knee injury, and has been building ever since.

The 23-year-old signed a deal to move from A-League Women's club Sydney FC to Norway earlier this year and has impressed, scoring a goal and assisting another in her first seven games with the new club.

Former Sydney defender Tori Tumeth has also received a maiden call-up after shining for the Vancouver Rise in Canada's Northern Super League. At the same time, Melbourne Victory's Courtney Newbon is the third potential debutant.

But the Australians will be without stars Alanna Kennedy and Charlize Rule due to injury, while Arsenal midfielder Kyra Cooney-Cross also won't join the team as she continues her return to football.

Midfielder Isabel Gomez and goalkeeper Ilona Melegh have been dropped after they were part of the side for their two-game series against Mexico in June.

Superstar Sam Kerr has been named to feature in the friendlies. (Getty Images: Dustin Satloff)

Defenders Charli Grant and Alexia Apostolakis, along with midfielder Daniela Galic, will return to the national team set-up.

European stars Mary Fowler, Caitlin Foord, Ellie Carpenter and Steph Catley have also been named, as well as Gotham City's Sam Kerr.

The October international window marks a crucial stage in the Matildas' preparation for the FIFA Women's World Cup, which gets underway in Brazil next June.

There are only a handful of international breaks before the showpiece tournament, meaning every game is crucial for Australia as they look to build on their fourth-place finish in 2023.

"We have a good mix of experience, players returning to the squad and players earning their first senior call-ups, which is important as we build towards the Women's World Cup," Montemurro said.

"We want to use these games to strengthen our connections, build confidence and continue developing as a team.

"Germany will test us against one of Europe's leading teams, while Haiti will provide a different style and perspective. Both will be valuable as we continue to prepare for the FIFA Women's World Cup."

title: From Kylie to Lachie, everything you need to know for the AFL grand final
text:
The 2026 AFL grand final is almost upon us, as the Brisbane Lions look to make history with their second threepeat in 25 years, and the Fremantle Dockers look to win their first flag since joining the league in 1995.

Here's everything you need to know about the game.

When is the 2026 AFL grand final?

The game starts 2.30pm (AEST) on Saturday, September 26 at the MCG.

That's 12.30pm for those watching in Western Australia, and 2pm for South Australia.

Which teams are playing in the grand final?

The Brisbane Lions are facing off with the Fremantle Dockers.

This is Brisbane's fourth grand final in a row, losing to Collingwood in 2023, before beating Sydney and Geelong in the following years.

Should they win, it would be the second threepeat in their history, following 2001-2003, and it would see them join Melbourne (1939-41 and 1955-57) as one of the only two teams to record the feat twice.

Meanwhile, Fremantle is yet to win a premiership after joining the league in 1995. This is the club's second grand final following its loss to Hawthorn in 2013.

Over their past six games against each other, the ledger is tied at 3-3, with the Dockers winning their most recent clash at the Gabba in round 13 this year.

How can you watch watch and listen to the grand final?

The game will be on Channel 7 and 7Plus, but be very aware that it will not be shown on Kayo or Fox Sports. It is the only game of the entire AFL season that is exclusive to Channel 7.

To listen to the grand final, join your local ABC Sport radio team, and follow along with the ABC Sport live blog at abc.net.au.

When will Kylie Minogue be performing?

Australia's pop princess should be on stage from about 1.30pm. Again, be very aware that Minogue's performance is pre-game and is not halftime entertainment. There is no halftime entertainment.

Other performers will be G Flip, musical actor Michael Paynter on the national anthem, and of course Mike Brady doing Up There Cazaly during the retiree motorcade.

The Wiggles will be performing at Friday's grand final parade through Melbourne.

Who will be lining up for the Lions and Dockers?

At this point we don't know.

Teams will be announced about 6pm (AEST) today, but before that we'll have to see if Lions superstar Lachie Neale's tribunal appeal against a one-match ban gets up.

ABC Sport's Andrew McGarry will be live blogging every moment of the appeal, with the case set to get underway at 4pm.

Should Neale miss out, Noah Answerth is the most likely player to come in for the Lions. The injured Brennan Cox is a chance to come in for the Dockers, but it looks odds on that the Dockers will be unchanged from their preliminary final victory over the Swans.

Who will present the cup to the winners?

The Lions have picked Simon Black, a Brownlow medallist and champion midfielder from that first threepeat, while the Dockers have gone with Shaun McManus, who debuted in Fremantle's inaugural season before playing 228 games.

title: Unemployment rate reaches post-COVID era high of 4.6pc in August
text:
Australia's unemployment rate drifted higher in August.

The national unemployment rate rose to 4.6 per cent, up from 4.5 per cent in July, in seasonally adjusted and trend terms.

It is the highest unemployment rate in the post-COVID era.

On Tuesday, RBA governor Michele Bullock said she thought an unemployment rate of somewhere between 4.5 and 5 per cent would "take enough heat out of the labour market" to ease pressure on inflation.

Rate rise looking likely All four major banks and the bulk of money market traders believe the Reserve Bank will raise interest rates next week and governor Michele Bullock did nothing to dissuade them during a speech in Sydney.

In recent weeks, all four major banks and the bulk of money market traders have also announced that they expect the RBA to lift interest rates next week to try to clamp down on economic activity and squash inflation.

Oscar Guth, economist for Oxford Economics Australia, said the higher unemployment rate should ease "some of the tightness" in the labour market but he still thought the RBA would lift rates next week.

Participation rate back near record high

The ABS data show that Australia's labour force increased by another 67,700 people in August, which pushed the participation rate up to 67.1 per cent, from 66.9 per cent in July.

That returns the participation rate to just below its record high of 67.2 per cent.

The labour force increased by 67,700 people last month because an extra 39,500 people found employment and an extra 28,200 people were recorded as being officially unemployed.

The RBA's post-COVID rate hikes caused Australians to work more The International Monetary Fund found that thousands of Australians took on a second or third job when the RBA hiked rates rapidly in 2022 and 2023. It expected the opposite.

The unemployment rate still increased, in that situation, because the growth in employment failed to keep pace with the influx of people into the labour force.

Earlier this year, a working paper published by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) found that the RBA's rapid rate hikes in the post-COVID era had seen the supply of labour increase in Australia, because many Australians in highly indebted households entered the workforce, or took on second or third jobs, to pay for their rising interest payments.

"This August we recorded a higher proportion of people who were previously not in the labour force moving to being unemployed, compared to recent years," Sean Crick, ABS head of labour statistics, said on Thursday.

CBA economist Ashwin Clarke said the increase in the participation rate last month was likely supported by the uptick in inflation and higher interest rates, "as households seek to recoup some of their lower real incomes by working more."

What do economists say?

David Bassanese, BetaShares chief economist, says the overall strength in employment will likely be "the final nail in the coffin" for the Reserve Bank to lift rates next week.

"For the RBA, the lift in unemployment will likely be regarded as unfortunate, but the price that needs to be paid to create more slack in the economy and lower domestic demand-driven inflation pressure," he said.

Interest rates back at 'sensible level' If you are struggling with current interest rates, the Reserve Bank's leaders delivered the sobering message that they are only just getting back to a "more sensible level".

"My base case remains that the RBA will raise interest rates by 0.25 percentage points next week to 4.6 per cent, with an even-odds chance of a follow-up hike on Melbourne Cup Day in early November."

EY senior economist Paula Gadsby said the data would do little to alter the interest rate outlook.

"The key challenge for the Reserve Bank is inflation, which has been outside the 2 to 3 per cent target band for some time," she said.

"A labour market that continues to absorb workers and support household spending indicates domestic demand pressures have not softened sufficiently to reduce inflation risks.

"At the same time, supply shocks in global energy markets are becoming more persistent and harder for the Reserve Bank to 'look through'.

"Today's result is unlikely to materially change the policy outlook, with financial markets pricing a 90 per cent probability of a rate hike [next week]," she said.

Citi economists Faraz Syed and Josh Williamson say they still expect the RBA to lift rates next week and again in November.

ACOSS says unemployment rate above 5 per cent would be a 'human disaster'

However, the Australian Council of Social Service (ACOSS), the peak council for community services nationally, has called on the RBA to try to keep the unemployment rate as low as possible.

Cassandra Goldie, ACOSS chief executive, said Australia's comparably low unemployment rate was a considerable achievement of the post-COVID era and we should not take it for granted.

"It must be protected," she said on Thursday.

Living on JobSeeker Calls for a boost to unemployment benefits have gone unheeded and experts say it is pushing job seekers into poverty.

"There is no question that increasing unemployment towards 5 or 6 per cent would represent a human disaster, with long-lasting damaging impacts for people unnecessarily locked out of the labour market and forced to rely on grossly inadequate income support payments."

She reminded policymakers that Jobseeker was now worth just 40 per cent of the minimum wage.

"The RBA should resist rate rises that would trigger further loss of the post-pandemic labour market gains," she continued.

"The government must now take the lead in managing inflation, with an emphasis on ensuring that inflation is reduced fairly and that people on low incomes are protected."

AI data centres and inflation

The rise in the unemployment rate comes as the RBA grapples with the inflationary impact of Australia's data centre construction boom.

On Tuesday, RBA governor Michele Bullock said AI would hopefully deliver great productivity benefits in the future but until then, the rush to build data centres was "adding" to short-term inflation pressures.

AI investment boom Australian data centre operators have raised a record $35 billion so far this year. Meanwhile, the RBA governor says central banks globally are monitoring the risk of an AI investment bubble.

Building data centres requires huge amounts of spending on construction, electrical infrastructure and skilled labour, as well as imported equipment such as advanced chips and servers.

Ms Bullock said that while AI investment was already adding to demand, there were "very few signs yet" that it was boosting the economy's supply capacity.

"AI is the great white hope to improve productivity," she said.

"But I think everyone also agrees that there are very few signs yet that AI is actually influencing the supply side of the economy [while] there's lots of evidence that it's influencing the demand side of the economy.

"So we've got this awkward sequencing event at the moment where, in Australia at least, we are in a situation of excess demand, and the AI boom is adding to that demand ahead of any potential supply impacts that it might have going forward."

Meanwhile, Victorian residents living just metres from a sprawling, hyper-scale data centre in Melbourne's west have called for remediation and financial compensation, including voluntary home buybacks.

This week a Senate inquiry on artificial intelligence and data centres heard from residents and local councils about the impact of an influx of data centres in Melbourne's west and north.

title: Analyst warns diesel could top $4 and rationing possible if US ban proceeds
text:
A leading energy analyst has warned that Australia could be looking at diesel rationing within weeks and prices topping $4 a litre if US President Donald Trump goes ahead with an export ban on the fuel.

MST Marquee's head of energy research Saul Kavonic said the proposed export ban was "probably the most worrying development we have seen in global fuel markets since the [Middle East] war began when it comes to Australia's vulnerability".

Mr Trump said on Tuesday, local time, he backed the idea of a ban on diesel exports from the US, which was being floated by some Republican politicians ahead of the midterm elections in November.

"I've said let's not send‌ out the diesel. ‌We make a lot of diesel … I've called for it. ‌I've called for it within my people," Trump told reporters before a meeting with the Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

The country exports roughly 1.3 million barrels of diesel a day, which is about one-quarter of its refining output.

Diesel prices have climbed to more than $US6.50 a gallon in the US, the highest average on record.

Loading...

Real threat of fuel rationing

Mr Kavonic told ABC's The Business program if the export ban went ahead, there was a very real risk of diesel fuel rationing in Australia and prices climbing 50 per cent to more than $4 a litre.

"If the US goes down this path, and particularly if they do it in a very severe way, I think we'll be looking at that in a matter of weeks," he said.

While Australia does not directly import diesel from the US, the flow-on effect on global markets puts Australia in a uniquely vulnerable position.

The economy is heavily weighted toward both agriculture and mining, both industries that rely heavily on diesel.

"Australia is actually the largest importer of diesel in the world; that's not per capita; that's an absolute sense," Mr Kavonic said.

Diesel 'crack spread' filling oil refiners' coffers The "crack spread", or profit margin, on diesel is increasing as refiners capitalise on the Middle East conflict, and it's hurting the slim margins of Australia's farmers.

"We account for 1 per cent of the world's fuel demand, but 10 per cent of the world's seaborne diesel imports."

The crunch happened because, globally, both the conflict in the Middle East and Ukraine-Russia war have seen a number of major refineries taken offline.

Russia and China have also stopped exporting refined fuels as the crisis evolved.

That means the US has been picking up the slack in the diesel export market.

US considering partial or full diesel ban

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the US government was examining whether it was feasible to have a full or partial ban.

Mr Kavonic said any bans could force the Australian government's hand.

"This is the kind of thing which could have to see Australia reconsider our demand management and rationing program potentially go to stage 3 and stage 4," Mr Kavonic said.

Under Australia's National Fuel Security Plan, stage 3 includes "practical measures to reduce fuel demand" and level 4 includes plans to "direct fuel supply to ensure national supply is allocated fairly" and "prioritisation of fuel supplies at the local level", generally considered to be rationing.

Track the latest petrol and diesel prices around Australia See what's happening with petrol and diesel prices near you, updated constantly.

"Well, it was probably only a month ago that Australia and the Australian government thought we'd managed through the worst of this crisis and we could actually disband the fuel task force," Mr Kavonic said.

Since then, two critical developments have occurred: disruption to fuel coming through the Red Sea, and now a possible US export ban.

With attacks by Houthis on both the Saudi oil pipelines and Red Sea shipping, oil companies were turning to clandestine ship-to-ship transfers.

"So if the US does go down this [export ban] path, particularly if they do it in a very severe way, I think we'll be looking at [rationing] in a matter of weeks, particularly if we don't see a de-escalation in the Middle East occurring at the same time," Mr Kavonic said.

"And if that continues to escalate, plus a US export ban, that's the one situation which we were really fearing and hoping would not happen. And unfortunately, it could be on our doorstep."

Could rising oil prices and a new US tariff affect your business, industry or livelihood? Tell us your story here.

Stockpiles won't last forever

He said while Australia had solid fuel stockpiles, the nation could run out quickly.

"And particularly we're heading into a season now where we need that diesel for our agricultural part of our economy. So we can't afford many delays."

Australia is a huge importer of diesel because our agriculture and resources industries are heavily reliant on it. (ABC News: Laurissa Smith)

Mr Kavonic said it was critical the federal government continued its attempts to shore up supply from international partners like Saudi Arabia.

"I think government, and minister Bowen, but all the way up to the prime minister, really stepped up at the beginning of this conflict. We paid more, but it kept coming, and that's commendable," he said.

"We thought we were past the worst of this, but now these developments suggest there's actually no light at the end of the tunnel here.

"Given our global supplies of oil and diesel have been drawn down significantly this year, and clearly there'll be increasing competition from other countries as well for the supplies that remain, we're still far from being out of this conflict.

"We have to keep up with this diplomatic engagement, and we might even have to look to re-arm, stand up that fuel task force if things continue to get worse from here."

While the US's complex supply chain means any export ban could also have internal ramifications, Mr Kavonic said it was still a possibility it could happen in the short-term to ease pressure on prices inside the country ahead of the midterm elections.

"The concern here is that they'll do this even if it's just temporarily, even if it's not sustainable, for political reasons, and then the rest of the world's going to pay the price in that near term."

Export ban could actually lead to internal fuel problems

Mr Kavonic is not alone in his view.

Capital Economics chief climate and commodities economist David Oxley said any ban could paradoxically force American refiners to cut supplies of oil products.

"While an export ban would initially boost the availability of domestic diesel supply to parts of the US, it would subsequently reduce the supply of diesel and other oil products because refining and distilling a barrel of crude oil produces a mix of products in closely fixed ratios.

Loading...

"Accordingly, if refiners can't sell or store the diesel that they produce, they'd eventually be forced to cut their overall output, including of gasoline and jet fuel."

Looking at the US Gulf Coast alone, Capital Economics estimates that "diesel storage in the Gulf could rise to pandemic-era highs" because of a sharp fall in refinery utilisation, "within a matter of weeks".

"All told, the political aspect of being seen as doing something to help reduce fuel prices in the run-up to the midterms means that some form of export restriction now seems likely to be announced in the coming weeks," Mr Oxley said.

"This would further complicate the outlooks for energy markets and fuel price inflation.

"We suspect that it would be short-lived."

title: Public pool at centre of fight to change 'appalling' disaster policy
text:
It was not so long ago that residents of Wingham, on the NSW Mid North Coast, feared their only public pool might close due to mounting maintenance costs and dwindling attendance numbers.

Then came a record-breaking flood, which took the decision out of everyone's hands.

The pool suffered severe structural damage as 700 millimetres of rain fell on Wingham and Taree in May 2025, cracking and damaging its foundations, plumbing and reticulation system as the flood-soaked soil moved beneath it.

The news was another blow to a devastated community, as they realised what they had lost.

"The fact the pool was destroyed, it had an effect on people's wellbeing," Mid Coast Mayor Claire Pontin said.

"I'm sure even the people who didn't use the pool felt the loss of it because it just dampened the mood, sorry for the pun, right across Wingham."

Wingham Memorial Pool suffered irreparable structural and underground damage. (ABC Mid North Coast: Marina Trajkovich)

Bob Clarke, who swam four days a week while the pool was open, said the health of the region's elderly had suffered since its closure.

"That's exercise I now don't get; but there are a lot of people that aren't getting that exercise," he said.

"It's a needed asset."

Bob Clarke used the pool four times a week while it was operational. (ABC Mid North Coast: Marina Trajkovich)

Loss of swimming lessons concerning

Kate Spriggs, whose father helped campaign for the community-funded pool in the 1960s, said its closure also meant many families in Wingham and surrounding communities were missing out on swimming lessons.

"There are families that have been able to travel to Taree, but we also know there's a significant proportion of our community who can't afford to travel," she said.

" It's just not viable for them. "

A group of passionate swimmers worked to keep the community pool repair campaign alive. (ABC Mid North Coast: Marina Trajkovich)

According to a Royal Life Saving Australia 2025 report, the swim skills of Australian children are declining.

The report found about half of Australian year 6 pupils were unable to swim a 50-metre pool lap or tread water for two minutes.

A 2024 study assessing the social value of Australia's pools also found they were crucial for community members of all backgrounds to connect and develop social connections, significantly improving people's health and wellbeing.

Locals say many families have gone without swimming lessons. (ABC Mid North Coast: Emma Siossian)

The situation galvanised the community, which embarked on a 16-month campaign to secure funding for a rebuild.

Last week, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced $15 million in state and federal funding for the project, which Ms Spriggs described as "fantastic news".

"Not only does the pool bring health benefits but it's the social connections that it brings to the community, an opportunity for people to spend time with each other … to bring other towns to the area," she said.

The Wingham Memorial Pool (bottom left corner) was badly affected by the flood. (Supplied: Mid Coast Council)

An 'appalling policy'

But while funding has now been secured, the fact the pool was not considered "essential public infrastructure" meant it was not immediately eligible for disaster funding.

Cr Pontin said she had spoken to federal Emergency Management Minister Kristy McBain about changing the classification.

"It's absolutely an appalling policy," she said.

Claire Pontin is advocating for better access to disaster relief funds. (ABC Mid North Coast: Marina Trajkovich)

The minister said feedback from councils would be considered, with a new local government taskforce discussing disaster funding challenges during their first meeting this week.

Cr Pontin said changes to the disaster categorisation system and new support package options for councils were also being developed in response to increased frequency and severity of natural disasters.

Anthony Albanese announced $15 million to rebuild the Wingham Memorial Pool, with Kristy McBain working on reforms to streamline disaster funding. (ABC News: ABC South East NSW: Floss Adams)

"The thing councils have spoken to me about is trying to streamline the process as much as possible," Ms McBain said.

"We know already that there is an audit process that the state requires and then there's a separate audit process that the federal government requires.

"We are working really closely with them … so councils can access that money quicker."

The minister said while securing funding for the Wingham Memorial Pool had been a "process", the correct steps had been followed to get "the right outcome".

Claire Pontin is calling for public pools to be classed as essential infrastructure. (Supplied: Isaac Goessling)

"In a disaster we have to get communities moving as soon as possible, which is why that essential public asset rebuild looks at roads and bridges to make sure communities remain connected," she said.

"But it is important we take those recreational assets into account."

Cr Pontin said the Wingham pool could be reopened by December 2027.

title: Meet this year's ARIA Award nominees
text:
This year marks the 40th anniversary of the ARIA Music Awards, and the nominees vying for the iconic pointy trophy this November have just been announced.

A host of Australian musicians, artisans and performers are lined up across 29 categories, following the induction of six legendary acts being inducted into the ARIA Hall of Fame earlier this year: Gurrumul, Jenny Morris, Kate Ceberano, Spiderbait, The Living End and Vika & Linda.

Who's got the most ARIA nominations?

Leading the pack, landing eight nominations each, are Genesis Owusu and Tame Impala.

Owusu's third genre-bending album, Red Star Wu & The Worldwide Scourge, has placed the Ghanaian-Australian rule-breaker in contention for Album of the Year, Best Solo Act and the public-voted Best Australian Live Act.

The 28-year-old's first two records each won Album of the Year, along with five additional ARIAs already in the trophy cabinet.

Tame Impala, aka West Australian polymath and 15-time ARIA winner Kevin Parker, extends a huge year behind fifth album Deadbeat, featuring the global hit Dracula.

On the eve of a national arena tour, Parker is up for Album of the Year, Best Solo Artist, and nominations in the Best Pop, Dance/Electronic and Alternative categories.

Genesis Owusu, Ecca Vandal among May's best albums From long-awaited comebacks to First Nations glam rock and genre-defying polymaths, May was stacked with excellent new releases.

Netting several impressive nods is first-time solo nominee Ecca Vandal. South African-born with Sri Lankan (Tamil) heritage and Melbourne-raised, her loud, empowering music mixes punk, neo-soul, metal, hip hop, and more.

Her second album, Looking For People To Unfollow, puts her in the mix for Album of the Year, Best Solo Artist and Breakthrough Artist.

Ecca Vandal, Genesis Owusu and Tame Impala all square off for an award returning for the first time since 2016: Best Alternative Release.

The category also includes Gang of Youths' comeback single Things Take Time and Meg Mac's fourth album It's My Party.

Who else is hoping for ARIAs glory?

Last year's breakout winner, electronic producer Ninajirachi, has scored five nominations.

So too has Yolŋu sensation Baker Boy, singing-drumming star G Flip, tough-talking independent indigenous woman Miss Kaninna, and soulful Australian-Samoan visionary Boy Soda.

Amyl & The Sniffers and Ninajirachi dominate 2025 ARIAs The ARIAs belonged to two relative underdogs this year. Don't know who they are? It's time to pay attention.

Clocking in with four ARIA chances each are pop auteur Troye Sivan, rock trio DMA's and Dom Dolla, the world-renowned DJ playing to 50,000-plus people at Marvel Stadium this month.

There is a host of iconic Australian musicians in the mix, too, including Paul Kelly, Vika & Linda, Keith Urban, Hilltop Hoods and impending Grand Final entertainer Kylie Minogue.

Elsewhere, The Wiggles face off against former member Emma Memma and a Bluey record for Best Children's Album.

The best music festival award is back for a second year, featuring CMC Rocks, Laneway, Spilt Milk, Victoria's Beyond the Valley and the Lismore leg of Groovin The Moo.

When are the ARIA Awards?

The winners will be revealed on Wednesday 18 November at a glitzy ceremony, hosted at Sydney's Hordern Pavilion on Gadigal Land and broadcast on Paramount+ and 10.

title: Golden Dragon Palace
text:

The coronated king of Melbourne’s south-eastern yum cha belt is well-known to committed fans, sending out its first steamer basket in 2002. Today, up to nine trolleys circle Golden Dragon Palace’s 200-seat room, carrying ethereally translucent prawn and chive dumplings, and rich and giving scallop siu mai.

Beautifully pleated and with fragrant fillings, their thin pliable wrappers are steamed into lilting softness. Hit the caramelised turnip cakes and those slippery cheung fun filled with barbecue pork. The a la carte dinner menu is a heavy tome listing endless things that can be done to king prawns and other big-ticket items.

It might seem retrograde, turning back to the polite Cantonese pomp of dim sum during this fiery, funky purple patch for regional Chinese food in Melbourne. But this Palace has a gravitational pull that lures cars down the Eastern Freeway at will.

Best for: A dazzling death-row meal with the nearest and dearest.

title: Gojo Ethiopian Cafe
text:
Every restaurant featured in The Age Good Food Guide 2026 in Melbourne’s Western Suburbs. See all stories .

Eating at Gojo awakens all your senses, and the recommended way to set them fully ablaze is with the mahberawi. Best shared between two or three, it’s a cost-effective, hands-on introduction to some of Ethiopia’s greatest hits. Giant injera, Ethiopia’s legendary sour flatbread, is piled with a mountain of meat and legume-based stews, colourful pickled vegetables, salad and extra injera.

Tear off pieces of the holy, holey carb, and use it to scoop up the peppery sauteed-lamb sensation that is awaze tibs. It’s also useful to clasp a fistful of doro wat, the chicken and boiled egg stew earthy with berbere and sprinkled here with homemade cheese.

The post-meal traditional coffee ceremony is a must. You’re shown the coffee beans roasting in a pan before they’re ground, brewed and poured from a jebena pot, while incense burns at your table beside a basket of sweetened popcorn.

Good to know: Pick up a spicy beef sambusa or two from the pie warmer at the counter on the way out.

A sheath of bubbly cheese heralds baked fusilli in a spicy-sweet sugo, while the crackly skin of pan-fried barramundi is a textural foil for its fork-tender flesh. Settle in anywhere at this dumpling bolthole and witness the precision pinching happening in the open kitchen. There, a fleet of composed Aunties roll and fill perfectly supple dough with the flavours of Northeast China and beyond. Begin with the satiny Sichuan wontons.

Plump with pork and prawn, and topped with fish roe, they arrive swimming in slurpable chilli oil that’s a thrilling fight of red chilli, Sichuan peppercorns, hot oil and sesame seeds. Tame the fireworks with egg and chive boiled dumplings dragged through soy and black vinegar.

Sides are equally rewarding: sesame oil-glazed cucumber salad and mild strands of shredded bean curd are both fresh accompaniments for golden-bottomed, pan-fried dumplings packed with pork and pickled cabbage. Grab yourself a suan mei tang, China’s addictive smoky plum drink, sit back and enjoy the dough to a soundtrack of sweet mainland Mandopop.

Must-order: Spicy stirring wontons.

If Kisume is Japanese-inspired dining with the volume turned up, the Chef ’s Table – a horseshoe-shaped bar upstairs for a handful of guests – turns it up to 11. We’re not talking noisy. We’re talking extra.

Instead of, say, a picture of Mount Fuji, you’ve got a woman posing for provocateur photographer Nobuyoshi Araki (a different take on the Japanese art of restraint, if you will).

The 16-course tasting menu isn’t afraid of fun. There’s chawanmushi and elegantly draped nigiri of hapuka, kingfish and alfonsino. But there’s also scallop in beurre blanc dotted with caviar, a gorgeous little sando of golden scampi fishcake and tartare sauce, and duck expertly roasted on its crown with a flattering accent of sansho and mandarin.

Every diner has a phone at the ready, and the chef plays it to the nines – or right up to 11.

In some respects Kylie Minogue has been preparing her entire life for the set that has brought Melbourne to a pink-tinged standstill this week. “They’re getting a show,” she said at the MCG on Thursday morning when asked what the 100,024 people at the sold-out AFL grand final, and the many millions watching at home, in pubs and at barbecue gatherings around the country, could expect from her pre-game on Saturday. “We really are throwing everything at it. They’re getting a Melbourne girl performing in her hometown, which is wild to me.” Kylie Minogue appeared at a media call at the MCG on Thursday ahead of her pre-game show at this weekend’s grand final. Joe Armao In some respects, though, she’s only just begun to get her head around what it means. Stepping out onto the hallowed turf for a rehearsal without amplification, with just her backing singers by her side, “it just struck me … I’m singing centre stage at the MCG. I just had that little moment for myself, which was amazing and a beautiful emotion.” “I’m hoping I don’t get too overcome with emotion – I might,” she added, urging herself to “hold it together, hold it together”.

Advertisement

Minogue has played plenty of stadiums in her 38-year career as a global pop music star. But she’s never played one in which she has to get on and off the stage in such quick time, rattle through a tight set, and make it coherent for a massive audience on live TV as well as those in the stands. “With a longer show, you might have two or three songs to kind of settle in, but with a 20-minute set, I’ve got to get to that point quickly,” she said. “But I did feel when we were rehearsing that as much as the MCG is gargantuan – and even when it’s empty it has this incredible energy – it’s also like a massive hug. It’s such a communal space that it did feel good out there.” The AFL has been trying to woo Minogue for years. This year, she said, just felt right. Joe Armao There’s also the small matter of the weather to contend with – “is it going to be gale force winds? Is it going to be boiling hot? Is it going to be pouring rain,” Minogue pondered. “But that’s part of the fun, isn’t it?” (For the record, Saturday is predicted to be cold, around 15 degrees, and wet, up to 15 millimetres of rain, not ideal for a performer with a penchant for Vegas-style costumes and slick dance moves.)

Advertisement

She declined to reveal what songs she would play, though she did reveal that Love At First Sight might be the one she most enjoys performing. But she promised a set of “songs that people know, a little bit of nostalgia, a little bit of fun, a few surprises”. She did hint, however, that there would be a nod to her own very Melbourne, very personal story in the set. “It makes a nice little mention of me being a young girl going to Camberwell High School and dreaming about pop music and what I might do in life, getting to the end of HSC – I’d already started acting, so there was nothing at school that made any sense to me. And then the question of what do you want to do, how are you going to live, how are you going to pay your bills, and just how far I’ve come, I guess, and it’s led me back to centre stage at home in the most iconic venue for the most iconic game, an Australian game. There’s just so much about this moment for me that’s hard for me to grasp, so I’m kind of in awe and wonder myself at this moment.” In one of her many pre-match social media appearances this week – really, whatever the AFL is paying her, they are getting serious bang for buck – Minogue was coached in how to kick a footy by Hawthorn players Nick Watson and Jack Ginnivan, aka The Wiz and Ginni. And it seems she got way more than on-ball advice from the exchange.

“We were talking about stepping over the line, and I’ve been thinking about a lot of those parallels,” she said. “I’m not in a team sport, but I kind of am. There’s so many people working on this show, and everyone’s got each other’s back, and the self-talk in your brain, in your mind, leading up to any important gig or game – ‘you can do it, you can’t do it, this is going to go wrong, that’s going to go, what if, but maybe’ – and I just felt a nice kind of oneness with people from a completely different field.” Related Article NRL 2026 Tones and I offered NRL grand final show only three weeks ago The doubts are just part and parcel of playing on the biggest stages, she added. “The voices in your head ... we’ve all got the same thing. For you guys, it’s probably when you get up the race and you step onto the field everything changes. “Same for me,” she said. “It’s like, ‘OK, there’s no turning back now. title: Chef Wong
text:

Even in Hong Kong, the home of dim sum, there’s a decline in dumpling masters devoting themselves to the art of yum cha. Let’s be grateful, then, for this restaurant, powered by a belief in honouring legacy, in this case that of Wing Kwong “Chef” Wong, a dim sum master who died last year, aged 70, after more than 50 years filling and folding dumplings. Wong’s daughter, Doris, now carries the torch.

Diners mark up the one-page order sheet with their choice of dumplings (all under $4; their folding precise and the fillings pert) through to XO fried rice and exemplary egg tarts. The rich meat of the house invention, coriander and roast duck, is brightened with prawn, while roast pork cheung fun are silky but properly chewy.

No shortcuts, no compromises. This is a modest restaurant, but there’s nowhere in Melbourne making dumplings with more integrity. What a gift.

Good to know: You can grab some of the excellent dumplings and fluffy pork buns from the freezer to take home.

Manhattan’s current program at Hook Lake is designed to build on a historical 1980s non-JORC-compliant resource at Jaws of 3.4 million tonnes at 2.38 g/t gold for about 285,000 ounces. The company’s recent drilling has consistently delivered thicker, higher-grade intercepts than the historical work, including a stunning 41.15-metre hit at 4.66g/t gold, featuring a spectacular 7.62m at 18.67g/t gold. Rice plays a starring role in Bangladeshi cuisine, and it’s done in two different ways for kacchi biryani and khichuri. In kacchi biryani, saffron-stained grains blanket lamb so soft you could whisper it off the bone. Khichuri boasts turmeric-yellow rice and chicken with a slow-building spice.

Dessert? Mishti doi – home-made pot-set yoghurt with rich caramel notes. Mango lassi is great, but borhani is a revelation: a salty, spicy yoghurt-based drink that’ll leave a green chilli calling card at the back of your throat. Service is warm if a little absent-minded but the food speaks for itself.

Must-order: Layers of fall-apart lamb, soft potato and fragrant rice make the kacchi biryani a crowd favourite for good reason.

A brilliantly hued tumble of heritage beetroot with creamy stracciatella; a virtuous side of chopped broccoli tossed with freekeh, almond and snipped herbs; and a dome of sticky date pudding with rivers of butterscotch sauce and fresh cream.

The place is perpetually packed and slightly on the pricey side (hello $110 club steak), but you can bring anyone – from a promising date to a fussy grandparent – and they’ll be content.

Must-order: Whipped cod roe dip with grassy olive oil and fingers of toasted flatbread.
