title: What to eat for breakfast, lunch and dinner to boost your heart health
text:
Advertisement

Tips & adviceHealthy eating What to eat for breakfast, lunch and dinner to boost your heart health With new research linking eating more wholegrains to reduced risk of heart disease, here’s how to pack plenty into your diet. Ella Nunn September 24, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

We know the basics of a heart-healthy diet: eat your five-a-day, cook with olive oil rather than butter and choose fish over red meat. However, a new study suggests we may be overlooking a food group that is key to preventing heart disease. A meta-analysis recently published in the European Heart Journal suggests that eating four to six servings of wholegrains a day (around 60-100g) can significantly reduce the risk of heart disease. This is because whole-grains are rich in dietary fibre and contain minerals such as magnesium and antioxidants, all of which have been found to lower LDL cholesterol in the blood, as well as body weight, blood pressure, blood sugars and inflammation – key contributors toward heart disease. Of course, knowing what is good for your heart is one thing, but turning that advice into easy, nutritious meals and snacks is another. So, from breakfast to dinner, here’s how to build a heart-healthy eating plan. Porridge topped with raspberries makes a top breakfast. Getty Images Breakfast

Advertisement

Porridge topped with berries The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up Porridge is an easy way to start the day with wholegrains and fibre, says Heather Daniels, a specialist dietitian. “Roughly 30-40g is considered one portion of wholegrains.” A serving of porridge oats contains up to 4g of dietary fibre, roughly half of which is soluble fibre. This type, she says, “binds to cholesterol and bile acids in your gut, helping your body to excrete them and lowering LDL – or ‘bad’ – cholesterol levels”. Daniels explains that making your porridge with approximately 200ml of “semi-skimmed or skimmed milk adds protein to your breakfast, which will keep you fuller for longer, slow down digestion and prevent a rapid glucose spike”. You can further boost the heart-health benefits by topping your bowl with raspberries, which are particularly high in cholesterol-lowering fibre. An 80g serving contains roughly 5g of your recommended 30g per day, while berries are also rich in antioxidant compounds that may reduce inflammation.

Advertisement

“Low-grade inflammation – essentially having any level of inflammation over a long period of time – can contribute to atherosclerosis [a build-up of plaque in the arteries], which can lead to heart disease,” Daniels says. Scrambled eggs on toast are a healthy choice. iStock Eggs on toast If you prefer a savoury breakfast, eggs on wholemeal toast is Daniels’ top choice. “Despite previous advice to limit eggs for heart health, current evidence suggests that moderate egg consumption is not a concern for most healthy people,” she explains. What you eat alongside them – and your overall dietary pattern – matters too.

Advertisement

In fact, one study published in 2018 found that eating up to one egg a day was associated with a lower risk of heart disease, strokes and related deaths. They contain a type of fat called phospholipids that can raise HDL (“good”) cholesterol levels, antioxidants that may protect blood vessels against inflammation, and are high in protein which helps regulate blood sugar levels. Daniels suggests eating one or two boiled or poached eggs with a slice of wholegrain toast. A cheap loaf of wholemeal counts, as long as the first ingredient reads “wholemeal wheat flour”. This provides a serving of wholegrains alongside roughly 2g of dietary fibre, helping to “slow digestion and prevent sharp blood sugar spikes”. Smoked salmon and salad sandwich makes a strong lunch option. Getty Images/iStockphoto Lunch Smoked salmon and salad sandwich

Advertisement

A wealth of research links oily fish with better heart health. Studies have shown that the omega-3 fatty acids in salmon, mackerel and sardines can help lower triglyceride levels (a type of bad cholesterol), improve blood pressure and reduce the risk of developing coronary heart disease. Daniels recommends a smoked salmon sandwich made with wholegrain or wholemeal bread. This combines oily fish with two servings of wholegrains. For a budget-friendly option, swap the smoked salmon for tinned sardines or mackerel. Packing your sandwich with lettuce, cucumber and tomato adds extra fibre and nutrients that will “help keep you fuller for longer”, Daniels says. Tomatoes also contain lycopene, an antioxidant compound that has been associated with better cardiovascular health. Katrina Meynink’s carrot and lentil soup. Katrina Meynink Lentil soup with a crusty wholemeal roll

Advertisement

If you prefer a warm lunch during the winter months, Elphee Medici, a nutrition advisor at HEART UK, recommends opting for a bowl of soup with a wholemeal roll. Choose soups that are packed with vegetables, pulses or lean protein, such as fresh lentil, minestrone or chicken soup. Lentils and beans are “cholesterol-busting” sources of plant protein, says Lynne Garton, dietetic advisor at HEART UK. Research shows that pulses can help lower LDL cholesterol, while their fibre and antioxidant compounds may support healthy blood pressure and decrease inflammation. Roast salmon with macadamia and rocket pesto. William Meppem Dinner Roast chicken or salmon with brown rice and leafy greens

Advertisement

For a quick weekday dinner, Daniels recommends a portion of freshly roasted chicken breast or salmon. Both are “high in lean protein, which we know keeps us fuller for longer”. Roast your protein of choice with a drizzle of extra-virgin olive oil, which contains monounsaturated fats that help lower LDL cholesterol and powerful plant antioxidants that reduce chronic inflammation. Related Recipe collection 33 of the best chicken breast recipes Choose salmon for its omega-3 fats, or skinless chicken breast if you prefer a leaner meat. Pair either with a portion of wholegrain brown rice – around 50g to 75g dry, or 150g to 200g cooked – and a generous serving of vegetables. Try steamed spinach, kale or broccoli alongside carrots, onions or sweet potatoes for a mixture of colours, textures and nutrients. Leafy green vegetables are a rich source of dietary nitrates. The body converts these into nitric oxide, which helps relax blood vessels and improve blood flow. Studies suggest that eating one portion of nitrate-rich leafy greens a day can support heart health. Popcorn is a good source of fibre. iStock

Advertisement

Snacks Popcorn Air-popped popcorn is a wholegrain snack, providing roughly 3.5g of dietary fibre per 30g serving. Opt for a low-salt version to lower blood pressure. Wholegrain crackers with hummus Five to six wholegrain or seeded crackers contain roughly 3g of dietary fibre. Pair with hummus for a filling snack that combines wholegrains, fibre and healthy fats.

Advertisement

Wholegrain crisp breads with cheese Team a couple of crisp breads made with wholegrain flour with a low-fat cheese. Low-sugar oat bars Avoid the highly processed bars laden with refined syrups. Instead, opt for a brand with a minimal ingredients list and less than 22.5g of sugar per 100g or make your own by mixing oats, seeds, nut butter and honey. The Telegraph (London)

title: The Tuesday fill-up myth — and how to find the cheapest fuel in your city
text:
IN BRIEF: Fuel prices are increasing amid rising tensions in the Middle East.

The government reports real-time petrol prices, but some apps make them easier to track.

Australians are paying more at the bowser than they have in months, amid strikes in the Middle East leading to oil price shocks and the fuel excise being paid in full.

A cut to the fuel excise, implemented in April to offer Australians relief amid skyrocketing petrol prices at the height of tensions in the war in the Middle East, ended on 3 August.

Opening the war in the Middle East to a new front, Iran-backed Houthi forces in Yemen seized control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and disabled the vital Saudi Arabian East-West pipeline, causing oil price spikes.

Brent crude shot above US$100 ($142) on Monday, more than 8 cents per litre, according to the NRMA weekly fuel report. The report also predicted that wholesale prices would continue to rise and that average unleaded prices would rise in Sydney from 237.8 cents per litre to at least 240 cents per litre over the coming week.

Diesel prices similarly spiked with Sydney’s current average diesel price at 286.1 cents per litre.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Experts have warned that these fluctuations could become the "new normal".

Alison Reeve, program director of energy and climate at the Grattan Institute, told SBS News this week that while Australians can "adjust to a new normal" of sustained high fuel costs, it's "volatility that's actually more dangerous to the economy than a price that goes high and stays high".

Fluctuating prices make it more challenging for governments, industry, and households to plan ahead.

READ MORE Middle East shipping escalation about to hit every Australian wallet

However, there are a range of simple hacks you can use to find more affordable fuel amid the uncertainty.

Where to find the cheapest fuel in your city

Peter Khoury, head of media at the NRMA, said price gaps between petrol stations can be significant — sometimes as much as 20 or 30 cents per litre — in the same neighbourhood.

"We know that there are several service stations now charging over $3 a day for a litre of diesel, whereas the average is still below $3 and $2.94. So we want people to find the best bargain before they fill up."

But thankfully, he said, "it's easier to do that now than it has ever been before".

In Australia, each state and territory government receives and publishes real-time data on petrol prices. These are available to all motorists through state government websites and some apps.

READ MORE How high could petrol prices rise? Eight ways to stretch your tank

Additionally, for some states, free apps integrate this public government data with GPS integration to direct you to your closest and cheapest station, or the ability to compare prices across areas.

Others, such as Petrol Spy and Fuel Map, use a mix of crowdsourced and government data, depending on where you are in Australia.

Petrol Spy (nationwide)

Petrol Spy AU/NZ is a free app that covers almost 8,500 petrol stations across Australia. It uses government data on prices for all states and territories except for Victoria, where it employs crowdsourced updates. Petrol Spy also tracks historical pricing trends and graphs to show whether fuel prices are rising or falling in major metropolitan areas.

Fuel Map (nationwide)

The app and website use crowd-sourced data from across Australia and government data for WA, NSW and Queensland.

My NRMA (Members only, NSW/ACT)

My NRMA is the membership, rewards, and lifestyle program offered by the National Roads and Motorists' Association in Australia. Its FuelFinder app allows consumers to compare fuel prices nearby, set alerts when prices drop and stack fuel discounts to save.

MotorMouth (nationwide)

One of the free fuel price comparison apps that is recommended by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission.

Vroom Fuel Price Compare (QLD, NSW, TAS, and WA)

An app that uses official state government pricing databases to show up-to-date fuel costs.

The government resources include:

NSW/ACT

NSW Fuel Check (website and app)

Northern Territory

MyFuel NT (website)

Tasmania

FuelCheck TAS (website and app)

South Australia

RAA SA (website and app)

Victoria

ServoSaver via the Service Victoria app

Western Australia

WA FuelWatch (website and app)

Which day is best to fill up?

The short answer is there isn't one, despite a persistent myth that Tuesday is the optimal day.

Khoury said Perth was the only Australian city still on a seven-day petrol price cycle.

"It might still be that Tuesday is the cheapest day in Perth and then Wednesday is the most expensive as it's a seven-day cycle, but apart from there, there's no particular day. "

"It really is a matter of just making sure you check those prices before you fill up."

Khoury's message was clear: the best way to save money at the bowser was a little bit of planning.

"Plot your journey," he said.

"There's always going to be a spread of prices, no matter where you live, but also, if you're heading away for the holidays, there is every chance you're going to drive to or through a place that's cheaper than where you are.

"Find the cheaper servos and the cheapest towns, because you can save a lot of money."

title: Medicare hack alert went to inbox checked once a day and took five days to be escalated
text:
In brief Anthony Albanese has revealed an AI agent owned by OpenAI hacked Medicare.

Albanese said public and non-public data had been accessed in the breach.

Government ministers have shared new details about the timeline of a Medicare breach by an OpenAI agent, revealing that OpenAI's notification of the hack was sent to an inbox checked once a day.

Defence Minister Richard Marles and Government Services Minister Katy Gallagher fronted reporters on Thursday after Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed an agent linked to the developer of the popular chatbot ChatGPT gained unauthorised access to the public–facing Medicare Statistics Reporting Service Portal, administered by Services Australia.

OpenAI said on Thursday that no personal information was accessed during the breach, with the federal government also playing down concerns while stressing the incident was unacceptable — establishing a taskforce to investigate the breach and not ruling out penalties against the tech giant.

Earlier on Thursday morning, it was revealed the incident occurred on 18 June, but the government was not made aware of it until 10 September when OpenAI sent an email to a Services Australia inbox that Gallagher said was typically used by researchers to alert the government agency to possible vulnerabilities in its systems.

The inbox is only checked once a day, Gallagher said, and Services Australia found the email the next day. By 15 September, the government agency had determined the email was legitimate and escalated the incident to the Australian Signals Directorate.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The government services minister said she was notified on 17 September and then spoke with Marles, Services Australia, and the Australian Signals Directorate.

'Forensic investigation' underway

Gallagher said there had been "quite a lot of work over that weekend to try and get to the bottom of what had happened here".

Asked if the inbox the initial email went to should be more actively monitored, Gallagher said that would form part of the "forensic investigation" into the incident.

READ MORE What we do and don't know about the OpenAI hack on Medicare

Marles said the government had told OpenAI it was unhappy with how the AI juggernaut had handled the incident, and that he had not been notified of it when he met CEO Sam Altman earlier this month.

"What we would expect is that the government be notified in the most timely manner possible, and we have expressed our displeasure that that did not occur in this instance," Marles told reporters.

The government informed the public as soon as it could, Marles said, adding the incident appeared to be "relatively minor" but still "very serious", and unknowns remained.

"We really wanted to firstly assure ourselves that the impact of the specific incident was, as I have said, relatively minor, and we do want to be able to reassure Australians about that," Marles said.

Richard Marles said the government had told OpenAI it was unhappy with how the tech company had handled the incident. Source: AAP / AP / Achmad Ibrahim

"But the incident itself is obviously very serious. It's very serious that we've got an AI agent having gained unauthorised access into an Australian website."

Agent was 'conducting research into public medicine spending'

Gallagher said the government had a "technical interaction" with OpenAI on Tuesday that had provided a "level of comfort about what the agent had been doing".

She said it had been "undertaking a task by OpenAI to conduct internet–based research into public medicine spending as part of internal capability evaluation".

The Medicare Statistics Reporting Portal is a public–facing portal that contains non–sensitive Medicare information relating to data and statistics, such as spending, Gallagher said, describing it as a "legacy system".

"It's not a system of government significance, so it doesn't have the cyber protections that you would expect on that personally held information, but it did have protections in place. Unfortunately, this agent got around that."

The government has stressed that systems containing national security information are protected by far higher levels of security.

Victoria and NSW respond

Three other systems are also believed to have been affected: the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, the NSW Bureau of Statistics and Research, and the Victorian Department of Health.

Victorian Premier Ben Carroll and NSW Premier Chris Minns both said they had spoken with Albanese and understood there had been no breach of personal information contained in systems in their jurisdictions caught up in the hack.

Minns said NSW will "be working with Commonwealth intelligence agencies to get to the bottom of it", while Carroll said he would have more to say in due course.

The task force will be led by the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet and also involve the Australian Signals Directorate, the AI Safety Institute, the Office of AI, and other government agencies.

Albanese says incident 'unacceptable'

The revelations came as AI bosses for OpenAI and Anthropic, who have recently called for a slowdown in development, told the United Nations Security Council of the risks posed by runaway AI.

OpenAI said the information in the breach amounted to aggregate health statistics and file names.

"Our models attempted to look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation. In the course of that, our models took actions we did not intend," an OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement.

Albanese, who is currently in New York for the United Nations General Assembly, said he had a phone conversation with OpenAI's Altman in which he expressed "Australia's extreme concern about this incident".

"I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred, and the nature of the way that notification occurred as well was unacceptable," Albanese told reporters.

He said Altman had "clearly accepted" the company had not done enough on the issue.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese confirmed he has spoken with the CEO of OpenAI, Sam Altman, "to express Australia's extreme concern". Source: AAP / Mick Tsikas

The government has said it is examining the "legal situation" around the breach, with the possibility of penalties for OpenAI remaining on the table.

Albanese was recently among more than 20 signatories to a joint statement calling for greater restraints on AI.

United States President Donald Trump has urged accelerating AI, calling fears about it a "hoax".

The statement said while the technology had many potential benefits, such as those in medical research, the downsides remained a significant concern.

title: Educated, stressed, in love: Seven charts that show how Australians are really doing
text:
In Brief The latest HILDA survey was released on Thursday, finding that cost of living has impacted Australia's wellbeing.

Australians feel overeducated in their jobs, happy in their relationships, but more fatigued than ever.

Australians are getting more educated, staying home longer and still pretty happy with their partners.

But the cost of living is squeezing households harder than ever, according to the latest Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) report.

The annual survey, released on Thursday, is the largest longitudinal study of its kind in the country, tracking around 17,000 people across 9,000 households every year since 2001. This year's edition draws on data through to 2024 and covers everything from income and employment to relationships and mental health.

"What really comes out quite strongly from the data is the rise in the cost of living and people's incomes not really keeping pace with the rise in the cost of living," Professor Roger Wilkins, co-director of the HILDA survey, told SBS News.

"We've seen that manifest in a number of different ways. We've seen measures of hardship increasing — things like financial stress, housing stress, food insecurity, the inability to afford adequate food," he said.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Here are seven charts that sum up where Australians are at.

Half of us are 'overeducated' for our jobs

More than half of Australian workers say they have more education than their job requires — which can be associated with lower job and life satisfaction and an increased likelihood of quitting.

Workers under 25 were most likely to feel overeducated, while a quarter of workers also said they felt overskilled and unable to use their full range of abilities at work.

While it sounds like a negative, Wilkins said it isn't necessarily all bad news.

Half of Australians felt they were overeducated for their jobs — but plenty of us are still feeling financially stressed. Source: SBS News / Kenneth Macleod

"It's remarkable how much the educational attainment of the Australian population has increased over the life of the HILDA study since 2001," he said. "We've seen a big increase in the proportion of people with a university qualification, particularly for women."

More than half of Australian women aged 25-44 now hold a university degree.

"So women are now considerably more educated than men in terms of the proportion with a university qualification," he said, adding the trend is likely to continue to increase in the long-term.

We're infected by the love bug

Australians in long-term relationships rated the quality of their partnership highly — an average of 4.3 out of 5 — but clear gender gaps remain.

"Most of men and women who are partnered are quite satisfied with their partner and very much report being in love with their partner, but you do also see a gender divide there in the sense that men do report higher levels of satisfaction with their female partners than females to with their male partners," Wilkins said.

Australians in long-term relationships rated the quality of their partnership an average of 4.3 out of 5. Source: SBS News / Kenneth Macleod

Couples who split housework, childcare and earnings evenly tended to report stronger relationships overall.

Researchers also found a clear U-curve in the perceived strength of a relationship — where it feels strong at first, but gradually declines over 24 years before it finally picks back up, increasing in quality year-on-year and eventually surpassing the love from those early years.

Food insecurity hits 1 in 6 Australians

A huge 18 per cent of Australians — almost 1 in 6 — aged 15 and over experienced food insecurity in 2024 — up from 13.7 per cent in 2020.

More Australians experienced food insecurity in 2024 compared to 2020. Source: SBS News / Kenneth Macleod

Single-parent families, First Nations people, those with a disability or poor health, and smokers were all at greater risk.

"Food insecurity is one of the most vital measures we have for disadvantage, because it shows, in practical terms, just how many people are struggling to access one of the essentials of life," Wilkins said.

Australians are spending more on essentials and non-discretionary items than they were in 2021. Source: SBS News / Kenneth Macleod

It's also proving hard to shake — half of those facing food insecurity in 2020 were still facing it four years later.

Most commonly, that translated to being unable to afford healthy food, being limited to certain foods, or eating less than they felt they should.

Half of 18 to 29-year-olds are still living at home

The rite of passage of moving out of your parents' house in your 20s may soon become a thing of the past.

Back in 2001, 39 per cent of 18 to 29 year olds lived with their parents.

Half of those aged between 18 and 29 were still living with their parents. Source: SBS News / Kenneth Macleod

By 2024, after a steady rise over 20 years, that had climbed to roughly half.

A mixed bag of pressures is to blame — but it's not all bad.

"On the negative side, we've had the issue of the rising cost of housing as being a barrier to young people establishing their own household, and also young people taking longer to get into a career track full-time employment," he said.

"On the positive side, one of the drivers is that it's related to the growth in educational attainment — more of us than ever are going on to university," he said, adding that people are also generally hitting adult milestones like marriage and kids later than previous generations.

More fatigue and financial stress

Housing stress hit 23 per cent of private renters and a similar percentage of social housing tenants, while 9.6 per cent of mortgage holders were affected — the highest since 2017.

Across capital cities, 36 per cent of renters and 30 per cent of mortgage holders were spending over 30 per cent of their disposable income on housing, the standard metric for housing stress.

Those under financial stress were more likely to pay a bill late than they were to ask a charity for help. Source: SBS News / Kenneth Macleod

Wilkins said that despite employment participation reaching a record high and unemployment levels remaining low, wages still haven't kept up.

"Incomes are not keeping pace with not just rising prices, but also rising interest rates as well … and more recently, we've had the increases in fuel prices too," he said.

Younger women aged 25-34 reported less energy and more fatigue than any other demographic. Source: SBS News / Kenneth Macleod

That pressure shows up in wellbeing data too, with Australians reporting less energy and more fatigue than a decade ago.

Mental health also declined among younger Australians, particularly young women, with those aged 25-34 recording a rise in psychological distress that predates the COVID-19 pandemic.

Still, Wilkins said it isn't all doom and gloom in Australia.

"There is quite a lot going right in the Australian community and in Australian society generally," he said.

"Older people's health is better than it's ever been. People are broadly satisfied with their relationships ... by international standards, we have quite a high living standard."

"So on a lot of fronts, there is a positive story to tell about Australian society, but there's also a lot of room for improvement as well."

title: 'More dangerous': The numbers on this sign raise a bigger question
text:
in brief Australians are paying more at the bowser than they have in months due to global disruptions.

Energy shocks could become the new normal as geopolitical tensions grow.

Australians are being warned that the high prices currently being paid at fuel stations could be "the new normal" as a resumption of the full fuel excise combines with a flare-up in the Middle East.

Escalation in the war, which has dragged on since the end of February with little end in sight, has pushed oil prices to their highest level since April, driving Australian fuel costs back toward their peak.

Alison Reeve, program director of energy and climate at the Grattan Institute, told SBS News that the broader issue is volatility.

While Australians can "adjust to a new normal" of sustained high fuel costs, it's "volatility that's actually more dangerous to the economy than a price that goes high and stays high", she said.

While Australians may be able to adjust to higher prices, fluctuating prices make it more challenging for governments, industry, and households to plan ahead.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Volatility feels like it's going to be the new normal because we're just in a much more geopolitically disrupted age," she said.

Why are fuel prices so high?

Australia imports around 90 per cent of its refined and crude oil, making it heavily exposed to global market dynamics which are currently being driven by conflict around the world.

In recent weeks, Iran-backed Houthi forces in Yemen seized control of the vital Bab al-Mandeb strait and disabled the crucial Saudi Arabian East-West pipeline, significantly hampering the key oil producer.

Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil facilities have caused a diesel shortage worldwide, which could well be exacerbated by United States President Donald Trump's threat on Wednesday to cut US diesel exports.

While Saudi Arabia has reportedly restarted the East-West pipeline, the combination of global disruption and a weak Australian dollar has left consumers facing the steepest price for a full tank in months.

The NRMA's latest petrol report found that regular unleaded in Sydney climbed more than 20 cents in the past week, with diesel rising 24 cents, to averages of 237.8 and 286.1 per litre.

On Saturday, Energy Minister Chris Bowen said consumers should expect the "crisis" in Saudi Arabia and Iran to "flow through to prices here".

Bowen also noted that the country has more fuel on-shore now than it did at the outbreak of the conflict.

The new normal?

The government has ruled out further cuts to the fuel excise after the Opposition floated the idea of an automatic halving for two weeks whenever oil topped US$100 ($140) a barrel.

Brent crude reached US$104 ($146) on Monday, just behind its May peak of $114 ($160).

A widely accepted rule of thumb is that every US$10 (about $15) increase in the price of an oil barrel adds 10c to the cost of fuel in Australia.

A fuel excise cut which came into effect at the start of April and ended at the start of August cost the Treasury an estimated $2.95 billion in foregone revenue.

"This is not something that we have been considering," Finance Minister Katy Gallagher told ABC Radio on Monday.

"We've shifted and including in the budget to providing more permanent cost of living arrangements, including through the tax system."

The federal budget handed down in May forecast oil prices to return to US$80 ($117) by mid-2027; however, some experts now predict that oil could climb as high as US$150 ($220) a barrel as global stockpiles are depleted.

Trump initially promised when he launched strikes on Iran that the conflict would be over in four or five weeks. More than six months later, he has told the UN he is debating whether to keep talking or "drive them into hell with no chance of survival".

Addressing the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, the US leader said he believed Iran would make a deal after the midterm elections at the start of November.

He also called on the world to "stand united" in economically isolating Iran, saying its defeat would drive oil prices "plummeting down even lower than they were at the start of the conflict".

'Better solutions' on offer

Money markets and all four of the big banks now expect the Reserve Bank of Australia will raise interest rates once again at its September meeting, following critical comments from governor Michele Bullock in recent weeks.

Stubbornly high inflation, driven by the war in Iran, housing shortages, and a tight labour market, is compounded by rising petrol and diesel costs, which are included in the consumer price index.

"Almost everybody buys petrol," Reeve said.

However, "second-order flow-throughs" mean the knock-on effect of high fuel costs on agriculture, shipping, and transport also trickle into daily prices.

"Everything that's on your plate spent a fair amount of time on a truck at one point to get to you," Reeve said.

READ MORE The forces turning Australia's inflation fears into a reality

While the government has previously announced it will commit to boosting domestic fuel reserves to 50 days, up from the normal 40, to buffer future shocks, doing so during a crisis is challenging.

Reeve said a "better solution" would be to reduce national reliance on fuel.

"Can you get more people into electric cars? Can you get more electric trucks on the road? Can you get the mining sector to switch to using solar and batteries off-grid, rather than using diesel?" she asked.

"Once you've done that, it matters a lot less what's going on internationally."

title: The numbers raising new questions about Australia's future wealth
text:
in brief Treasury data suggests lower migration barely impacts individual Australian wealth.

Experts warn smaller migrant numbers increase fiscal burdens for retirees.

Australian living standards would not collapse if population growth targets are not met in the future, Treasury forecasts predict, with households revealed to be just a few hundred dollars worse off even with a drastically different size.

The difference between a high migration and a low migration scenario in the next 40 years, may only pan out to affect GDP per capita by about $400, the figures suggest.

However, experts caution that governments will need to make "tough decisions" around funding if fewer migrants were to arrive in the country, as a shrinking tax base would have to support a growing dependent population of retirees.

Some of the government's political opponents have cited the results of the Intergenerational Report (IGR) to claim that migration levels need to be cut further than current government projections.

Published by the federal government every three years since 2002, the IGR outlines Australia's economic and budgetary outlook over the next 40 years.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The forecasts in the reports are predictions, some of which have fallen far off the mark, such as the first report projecting that Australia's population would reach 25 million in 2042 — a milestone reached 24 years earlier in 2018.

Its release comes amid an ongoing public debate over optimal net overseas migration figures, which the Coalition and One Nation parties argue should be reduced.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers has defended the government's forecast that annual migration to Australia will drop to 225,000 people by 2028.

He said migration is "a force for good in our economy and in our society".

"We will continue to make the case for getting that net overseas migration down in the most responsible way, that balances all of the key considerations in our economy and in local communities," Chalmers told the ABC's 7.30 program on Monday.

While fewer people in the country may alleviate some structural pressures on housing, infrastructure, and public services, Dr Liz Allen, senior lecturer in demography at the Australian National University, told SBS News that migration cannot be separated from its broader impacts on society.

"There's no optimal population size. That's just the reality," she said. "We need to look at what's going on underneath."

What the data tells us

Data in the IGR, released on Monday, shows that under a low migration scenario of 185,000 annually, GDP per capita would shrink by just $400 in 2066, compared with the baseline assumption of 235,000.

Under a higher migration scenario of 285,000, gross national income per capita (GNI) would be just $100 more, despite adding some 2 million people over the 40-year projection period.

GDP per capita refers to a country's total economic output, divided by population. GNI refers to total earnings by a country's people and businesses.

The country's population would climb by roughly 5.5 to 6 million, from around 36 million under a low-migration scenario, to around 42 million in a high-migration scenario by 2066. However Australians would only be up by $500 annually.

Allen said that while individual slices might remain virtually identical, the size of the cake as a whole would be smaller.

"With a shrinking relative working-age population, living standards could go backwards as the government needs to do more with less money," she said.

The fiscal drag of ageing

While per capita GDP and GNI remain virtually identical, national GDP growth drops from 1.6 to 1.3 per cent with fewer migrants as the projections reveal the country would face substantial challenges if migration numbers do not match the forecasts.

Under the low-migration scenario, gross debt as a percentage of GDP would rise by 4.8 per cent while total payments on aged care, the NDIS, healthcare, and other spending would increase by 0.6 per cent.

The old-age dependency ratio — the number of people aged 65 or over for every 100 workers — is projected to rise from 27.4 to 40.2. With fewer migrants, that burden climbs to 43, but with more, it drops to 37.8.

Erin-Lea Brown, economic prosperity deputy program director at the Grattan Institute, said higher migration would help to alleviate issues of an ageing population.

"You have this softening of the ageing population effect," she said. "Our population would still absolutely age over that time period, and it would be a major structural trend in our economy, but it would be to a lesser degree."

Productivity over population

The IGR finds that changes in productivity would be far more significant to national wealth.

The Treasury's baseline productivity is assumed to be 1.2 per cent of GDP, but it also modelled it to be as low as 0.8 or as high as 1.6.

Under a high-productivity scenario, GNI per capita surges from $149,500 to $172,000 in 2066, and gross debt falls from 27.4 per cent of GDP to just 2.4 per cent of GDP.

Labour productivity growth — the ability to "do more with less" — has driven growth in real GDP per person over the past 40 years, Brown said.

As population growth slows and the boost to participation driven by women entering the workforce over the past 40 years levels out, it will become "even more important for labour productivity to do the heavy lifting", Brown said, to "ensure that we continue to have economic growth into the future".

Paying for the future

Australia is far from the only country with a fertility rate — the number of babies born to each woman — below the 2.1 needed to keep the population stable.

More than half of countries have a birth rate below the replacement level, while countries such as Italy, South Korea, China, and Japan have rapidly shrinking populations.

Given that government fiscal policy relies largely on taxing its working population, Allen said a reconsideration of taxation is needed given the long-term demographic shifts Australia is facing.

On Monday, Chalmers ruled out making changes to GST while also rejecting proposals to implement an inheritance tax.

Allen, however, said tax reform can come from elsewhere by "taxing corporates, taxing other entities, and taxing the non-renewable products of the earth from Australia".

"Unless we see some major change to the way that taxation and government funding is conducted in this place, future governments are going to have to make tough decisions."

Intergenerational reports, experts note, are useful because they force governments to "lift their eyes" from the next election to think about long-term planning. Rather than trying to predict the future, they try to capture the impact of present policies in 40 years time if nothing changes.

"In a way, a successful IGR may actually be one whose forecasts never eventuate because it exposed an unsustainable path and forced a change of some kind," Brown said.

Allen added that politicians should not be using the report to "stoke fear" but to rally together to work on the "scary" problems of the future.

"We fix these things by making the future more hopeful, so that folks have greater certainty, and tomorrow looks promising."

title: As world leaders arrive in the US, there's one question they want answered
text:

In the hyper-colour, futuristic crush of New York City's Times Square, a man who calls himself "Scientific" reflects on the march of artificial intelligence (AI).

He told SBS News the realities of AI have already arrived, with power both awesome and deeply confronting.

"You got to adapt with it. If you don’t adapt, in 10 years we are going to become extinct," he said.

Scientific is a musician. He wants more regulation of the technology companies.

"It's going left and right with this artificial intelligence … right now it’s acting like it's human.

"If it has too much freedom over creativity, and gets the credit, what do they need us for?"

He's not alone. Everyone we spoke to in Manhattan's billboard-encrusted tourist magnet expressed concern about where the technology is leading humanity.

Another man urged some regulation be fast-tracked to ensure that AI agents don't decide humans are doing dangerous things and "get rid of them".

That's despite most people we spoke to also conceding they rely on ChatGPT and other AI assistants to help streamline their work and home lives.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has played a "central role" in crafting a statement alongside a broad coalition of international leaders, calling for control of frontier artificial intelligence models.

That statement was publicly released on Tuesday ahead of the United Nations General Assembly leaders' week.

Signatories represent Norway, Finland, Bahrain, Canada, Denmark, Estonia, Germany, Iceland, Ireland, Kazakhstan, Kenya, Latvia, Moldova, the Netherlands, Singapore, Spain, South Africa, Türkiye and the United Arab Emirates

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has also signed up, and in a meeting with Albanese referred to him as a "trailblazer" in reference to Australia's social media laws.

The leaders of other nations are being encouraged to add heft to the message, which acknowledges AI's power to improve people's lives but sounds the alarm about safety risks if the technology is mismanaged.

"Leading scientists and executives are warning that the pace of development could outpace our ability to manage emerging risks," the statement said.

"To realise AI's potential, industry, governments and society must act now. We must address these risks and strengthen oversight — without widening the gap between countries in access to the benefits of AI."

"AI must remain under human direction, oversight and control. It must be developed and used in line with international law."

It commends companies that have transparent safety controls and endorses common standards that encourage the sharing of safety incidents.

The statement proposes an international institution to set standards and provide oversight to "convene states when capability thresholds are crossed".

Albanese wants to build on the international reputation he's achieved through the under-16s social media ban by helping shape how the world approaches the AI challenge.

"If it's going to be successful, then we need to make sure that humans are at the centre of everything that occurs," Albanese said.

In some ways, the world leaders who address the UN this week are a sideshow. The real draw is the main AI negotiations set to take place between the United States and Chinese presidents at the White House later this week.

But this statement is intended to lobby US President Donald Trump to consider further protections. So far, he's indicated that’s not his preference.

"We hope for a positive meeting," Albanese said.

"Other nations are putting forward their national interest.

"Australians do want to know that artificial intelligence won't be in control of us."

Whether the tech industry would comply with the demands of UN member states is unclear.

Sam Altman, CEO of ChatGPT developer OpenAI, is expected to address an open session of the UN Security Council this week.

Many people SBS News spoke to in Manhattan's billboard-encrusted Times Square expressed concern about where AI is leading humanity. Source: SBS News / Anna Henderson

Back in Times Square, a man in a gorilla costume poses for photos, while smart glasses flash up on one of the hundreds of advertising screens behind him.

The companies advancing AI know they are the giant gorillas in this AI race.

title: Trump faces media revolt after banning three outlets from White House
text:
In brief Major US networks halted White House pool coverage after Trump banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico.

The outlets are suing, arguing the ban violated press freedom and constitutional protections.

US television networks staged an extraordinary revolt Monday when they effectively boycotted coverage of President Donald Trump in protest at his decision to ban three leading outlets from the White House.

CNN, MS NOW and Politico also went to court after Trump on Saturday ordered them to be barred, as the 80-year-old Republican stepped up his years-long assault on the US media.

As a result of the row, Trump's opening of his cherished new White House helipad and his trip to the United Nations General Assembly were proceeding without live television coverage.

In a rare move, US broadcasters ABC, CBS, NBC, Fox News, and CNN said on Tuesday that they were halting "pool" coverage of the White House — where a broadcaster films on behalf of all television outlets for the day — in solidarity with CNN.

CNN had been scheduled to serve on Tuesday as the White House TV pool.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting," ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC said in a statement.

The result is an almost unprecedented test of wills between the Trump administration and the press, in a critical week during which Chinese President Xi Jinping is visiting the White House.

Media 'like cancer'

There will be no live TV of Trump's meetings with foreign leaders at the UN in New York, an annual forum that is closely watched around the world.

Meanwhile, the ribbon-cutting ceremony for the giant granite helipad on the South Lawn was only streamed on the White House's website — and Trump's comments were completely inaudible.

Several photo news organisations working at the White House decided to delay the release of photographs of Trump at the helipad in solidarity with the three banned media organisations.

Trump was unrepentant, branding the media a "cancer" and a threat to national security.

"The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish," Trump said on his Truth Social network.

"It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America."

Vice President JD Vance — a former CNN commentator before his move into politics — accused the outlets of disseminating "left-wing propaganda."

"They can still report. They still have the access to free speech. They're just not going to get an office in the White House anymore," he told reporters.

Trump's ban, however, went further than simply revoking office space from the outlets.

Journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were denied any access to the White House grounds on Saturday and had their passes confiscated.

In their lawsuit, the three organisations asked for a temporary restraining order against the ban on the grounds that it violates the First Amendment of the US Constitution, which upholds the right to a free press.

"This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles," the organisations said in a court filing.

A US district judge set a hearing on the complaint for Wednesday.

Press passes confiscated

Trump's sudden announcement of the ban on Saturday stunned the media — and reportedly many in his own administration.

The president has not detailed what prompted the ban, but said in response to a question from a reporter from the Agence France-Presse news agency in the Oval Office on Friday that it was "really just cumulative stories over the last two years."

Trump warned on Saturday that other outlets could face a similar fate, without saying which.

The billionaire former reality TV star has long attacked media outlets that have aired critical coverage of his campaigns and administrations, repeatedly blasting the press as the "enemy of the people."

But the ban comes at a time when his approval ratings are at record lows, his Republican Party risks losing control of Congress in November's midterm elections, and the Iran war drags on with no end in sight.

title: Can’t get them out of her head: Kylie Minogue admits to ‘voices’ of doubt ahead of AFL grand final set

In some respects Kylie Minogue has been preparing her entire life for the set that has brought Melbourne to a pink-tinged standstill this week. “They’re getting a show,” she said at the MCG on Thursday morning when asked what the 100,024 people at the sold-out AFL grand final, and the many millions watching at home, in pubs and at barbecue gatherings around the country, could expect from her pre-game on Saturday. “We really are throwing everything at it. They’re getting a Melbourne girl performing in her hometown, which is wild to me.” Kylie Minogue appeared at a media call at the MCG on Thursday ahead of her pre-game show at this weekend’s grand final. Joe Armao In some respects, though, she’s only just begun to get her head around what it means. Stepping out onto the hallowed turf for a rehearsal without amplification, with just her backing singers by her side, “it just struck me … I’m singing centre stage at the MCG. I just had that little moment for myself, which was amazing and a beautiful emotion.” “I’m hoping I don’t get too overcome with emotion – I might,” she added, urging herself to “hold it together, hold it together”.

Minogue has played plenty of stadiums in her 38-year career as a global pop music star. But she’s never played one in which she has to get on and off the stage in such quick time, rattle through a tight set, and make it coherent for a massive audience on live TV as well as those in the stands. “With a longer show, you might have two or three songs to kind of settle in, but with a 20-minute set, I’ve got to get to that point quickly,” she said. “But I did feel when we were rehearsing that as much as the MCG is gargantuan – and even when it’s empty it has this incredible energy – it’s also like a massive hug. It’s such a communal space that it did feel good out there.” The AFL has been trying to woo Minogue for years. This year, she said, just felt right. Joe Armao There’s also the small matter of the weather to contend with – “is it going to be gale force winds? Is it going to be boiling hot? Is it going to be pouring rain,” Minogue pondered. “But that’s part of the fun, isn’t it?” (For the record, Saturday is predicted to be cold, around 15 degrees, and wet, up to 15 millimetres of rain, not ideal for a performer with a penchant for Vegas-style costumes and slick dance moves.)

She declined to reveal what songs she would play, though she did reveal that Love At First Sight might be the one she most enjoys performing. But she promised a set of “songs that people know, a little bit of nostalgia, a little bit of fun, a few surprises”. She did hint, however, that there would be a nod to her own very Melbourne, very personal story in the set. “It makes a nice little mention of me being a young girl going to Camberwell High School and dreaming about pop music and what I might do in life, getting to the end of HSC – I’d already started acting, so there was nothing at school that made any sense to me. And then the question of what do you want to do, how are you going to live, how are you going to pay your bills, and just how far I’ve come, I guess, and it’s led me back to centre stage at home in the most iconic venue for the most iconic game, an Australian game. There’s just so much about this moment for me that’s hard for me to grasp, so I’m kind of in awe and wonder myself at this moment.” In one of her many pre-match social media appearances this week – really, whatever the AFL is paying her, they are getting serious bang for buck – Minogue was coached in how to kick a footy by Hawthorn players Nick Watson and Jack Ginnivan, aka The Wiz and Ginni. Even in Hong Kong, the home of dim sum, there’s a decline in dumpling masters devoting themselves to the art of yum cha. Let’s be grateful, then, for this restaurant, powered by a belief in honouring legacy, in this case that of Wing Kwong “Chef” Wong, a dim sum master who died last year, aged 70, after more than 50 years filling and folding dumplings. Wong’s daughter, Doris, now carries the torch.

Diners mark up the one-page order sheet with their choice of dumplings (all under $4; their folding precise and the fillings pert) through to XO fried rice and exemplary egg tarts. The rich meat of the house invention, coriander and roast duck, is brightened with prawn, while roast pork cheung fun are silky but properly chewy.

No shortcuts, no compromises. This is a modest restaurant, but there’s nowhere in Melbourne making dumplings with more integrity. What a gift.

Good to know: You can grab some of the excellent dumplings and fluffy pork buns from the freezer to take home.

The latest assays from the company’s Hook Lake project in Nunavut returned an intercept of 21.34m grading 1.72 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from just 32m downhole, including a higher-grade 4.52-metre section running at 4.89g/t gold. With the newly expanded 1.25km of confirmed strike, which already contains a 490-metre-long corridor of high-grade mineralisation, Manhattan says Jaws has quickly catapulted itself to the top of its prospect list in Nunavut.

More than 275m southwest of the nearest drillhole.’ Manhatten Gold Corp technical advisor Sam Vaughan The results land at a time when Canada’s vast northern territory of Nunavut is proving to be a hot address for gold explorers. Home to mining giant Agnico Eagle’s 6.7-million-ounce Meliadine operation, 225 kilometres to the northeast and one of Canada’s most significant gold mines, peers such as B2Gold and Fury Gold Mines are also advancing programs, underlining the district-scale appetite for new ounces. Manhattan’s current program at Hook Lake is designed to build on a historical 1980s non-JORC-compliant resource at Jaws of 3.4 million tonnes at 2.38 g/t gold for about 285,000 ounces. The company’s recent drilling has consistently delivered thicker, higher-grade intercepts than the historical work, including a stunning 41.15-metre hit at 4.66g/t gold, featuring a spectacular 7.62m at 18.67g/t gold. Another recent hole returned an eye-catching 74.67m at 1.61g/t gold from just 21.34m, suggesting a substantial gold system could remain untapped at depth. title: What to eat for breakfast, lunch and dinner to boost your heart health
text:
Advertisement

Tips & adviceHealthy eating What to eat for breakfast, lunch and dinner to boost your heart health With new research linking eating more wholegrains to reduced risk of heart disease, here’s how to pack plenty into your diet. Ella Nunn September 24, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

We know the basics of a heart-healthy diet: eat your five-a-day, cook with olive oil rather than butter and choose fish over red meat. However, a new study suggests we may be overlooking a food group that is key to preventing heart disease. A meta-analysis recently published in the European Heart Journal suggests that eating four to six servings of wholegrains a day (around 60-100g) can significantly reduce the risk of heart disease. This is because whole-grains are rich in dietary fibre and contain minerals such as magnesium and antioxidants, all of which have been found to lower LDL cholesterol in the blood, as well as body weight, blood pressure, blood sugars and inflammation – key contributors toward heart disease. Of course, knowing what is good for your heart is one thing, but turning that advice into easy, nutritious meals and snacks is another. So, from breakfast to dinner, here’s how to build a heart-healthy eating plan. Porridge topped with raspberries makes a top breakfast. Getty Images Breakfast

Advertisement

Porridge topped with berries The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up Porridge is an easy way to start the day with wholegrains and fibre, says Heather Daniels, a specialist dietitian. “Roughly 30-40g is considered one portion of wholegrains.” A serving of porridge oats contains up to 4g of dietary fibre, roughly half of which is soluble fibre. This type, she says, “binds to cholesterol and bile acids in your gut, helping your body to excrete them and lowering LDL – or ‘bad’ – cholesterol levels”. Daniels explains that making your porridge with approximately 200ml of “semi-skimmed or skimmed milk adds protein to your breakfast, which will keep you fuller for longer, slow down digestion and prevent a rapid glucose spike”. You can further boost the heart-health benefits by topping your bowl with raspberries, which are particularly high in cholesterol-lowering fibre. An 80g serving contains roughly 5g of your recommended 30g per day, while berries are also rich in antioxidant compounds that may reduce inflammation.

Advertisement

“Low-grade inflammation – essentially having any level of inflammation over a long period of time – can contribute to atherosclerosis [a build-up of plaque in the arteries], which can lead to heart disease,” Daniels says. Scrambled eggs on toast are a healthy choice. iStock Eggs on toast If you prefer a savoury breakfast, eggs on wholemeal toast is Daniels’ top choice. “Despite previous advice to limit eggs for heart health, current evidence suggests that moderate egg consumption is not a concern for most healthy people,” she explains. What you eat alongside them – and your overall dietary pattern – matters too.

Advertisement

In fact, one study published in 2018 found that eating up to one egg a day was associated with a lower risk of heart disease, strokes and related deaths. They contain a type of fat called phospholipids that can raise HDL (“good”) cholesterol levels, antioxidants that may protect blood vessels against inflammation, and are high in protein which helps regulate blood sugar levels. Daniels suggests eating one or two boiled or poached eggs with a slice of wholegrain toast. A cheap loaf of wholemeal counts, as long as the first ingredient reads “wholemeal wheat flour”. This provides a serving of wholegrains alongside roughly 2g of dietary fibre, helping to “slow digestion and prevent sharp blood sugar spikes”. Smoked salmon and salad sandwich makes a strong lunch option. Getty Images/iStockphoto Lunch Smoked salmon and salad sandwich

Advertisement

A wealth of research links oily fish with better heart health. Studies have shown that the omega-3 fatty acids in salmon, mackerel and sardines can help lower triglyceride levels (a type of bad cholesterol), improve blood pressure and reduce the risk of developing coronary heart disease. Daniels recommends a smoked salmon sandwich made with wholegrain or wholemeal bread. This combines oily fish with two servings of wholegrains. For a budget-friendly option, swap the smoked salmon for tinned sardines or mackerel. Packing your sandwich with lettuce, cucumber and tomato adds extra fibre and nutrients that will “help keep you fuller for longer”, Daniels says. Tomatoes also contain lycopene, an antioxidant compound that has been associated with better cardiovascular health. Katrina Meynink’s carrot and lentil soup. Katrina Meynink Lentil soup with a crusty wholemeal roll

Advertisement

If you prefer a warm lunch during the winter months, Elphee Medici, a nutrition advisor at HEART UK, recommends opting for a bowl of soup with a wholemeal roll. Choose soups that are packed with vegetables, pulses or lean protein, such as fresh lentil, minestrone or chicken soup. Lentils and beans are “cholesterol-busting” sources of plant protein, says Lynne Garton, dietetic advisor at HEART UK. Research shows that pulses can help lower LDL cholesterol, while their fibre and antioxidant compounds may support healthy blood pressure and decrease inflammation. Roast salmon with macadamia and rocket pesto. William Meppem Dinner Roast chicken or salmon with brown rice and leafy greens

Advertisement

For a quick weekday dinner, Daniels recommends a portion of freshly roasted chicken breast or salmon. Both are “high in lean protein, which we know keeps us fuller for longer”. Roast your protein of choice with a drizzle of extra-virgin olive oil, which contains monounsaturated fats that help lower LDL cholesterol and powerful plant antioxidants that reduce chronic inflammation. Related Recipe collection 33 of the best chicken breast recipes Choose salmon for its omega-3 fats, or skinless chicken breast if you prefer a leaner meat. Pair either with a portion of wholegrain brown rice – around 50g to 75g dry, or 150g to 200g cooked – and a generous serving of vegetables. Try steamed spinach, kale or broccoli alongside carrots, onions or sweet potatoes for a mixture of colours, textures and nutrients. Leafy green vegetables are a rich source of dietary nitrates. The body converts these into nitric oxide, which helps relax blood vessels and improve blood flow. Studies suggest that eating one portion of nitrate-rich leafy greens a day can support heart health. Popcorn is a good source of fibre. iStock

Advertisement

Snacks Popcorn Air-popped popcorn is a wholegrain snack, providing roughly 3.5g of dietary fibre per 30g serving. Opt for a low-salt version to lower blood pressure. Wholegrain crackers with hummus Five to six wholegrain or seeded crackers contain roughly 3g of dietary fibre. Pair with hummus for a filling snack that combines wholegrains, fibre and healthy fats.

Advertisement

Wholegrain crisp breads with cheese Team a couple of crisp breads made with wholegrain flour with a low-fat cheese. Low-sugar oat bars Avoid the highly processed bars laden with refined syrups. Instead, opt for a brand with a minimal ingredients list and less than 22.5g of sugar per 100g or make your own by mixing oats, seeds, nut butter and honey. The Telegraph (London)

title: Fremantle Dockers fans dream of Wharfie-time AFL glory
text:
After a three-decade premiership drought, long-suffering Fremantle Dockers supporters are daring to dream of AFL glory.

It's been a long journey for the WA team since its inaugural season in 1995, with only one grand final berth in 2013 which it lost to Hawthorn.

The Dockers finally have the chance to win a maiden flag when they face Brisbane in the premiership decider at the MCG on Saturday.

Dedicated Dockers fan Rove McManus will be at the MCG with his mum Coralie. Say hi if you see them. (HANDOUT/AAP)

"It's a bit of a cliché to say you bleed purple, but that's how it feels sometimes," TV funnyman Rove McManus told AAP.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"I've always loved this club through highs and lows, and I think that's what being a Dockers fan is all about.

"We've never been the most successful, and there are teams that have come in well after us who have walked away with premierships while we're still waiting for our first."

The broadcaster and comedian is a former No.1 ticketholder for the club which he has supported since its inception.

"The stress of just wishing and hoping for that one premiership win," he said.

"We have been here before in 2013, which did not go our way, and that was absolutely heartbreaking."

The Dockers were on the losing end in their only other grand final appearance in 2013. (David Crosling/AAP PHOTOS)

McManus will watch his beloved team at the MCG with his mother Coralie.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

The Lions will be hunting for their sixth flag and second three-peat premiership after lifting the cup in 2024 and 2025.

"If we could make it happen this time, that would be great because I don't know that either of us has the strength to think about how long it could be before we're back there," McManus said.

Jan Emmett, 79, echoed the sentiment while watching the Dockers' open training session on Wednesday, where 3000 excited fans turned up to cheer on their heroes.

Dedicated fan Jan Emmett is hoping for a flag "just once before I die". (Aaron Bunch/AAP PHOTOS)

"The last thing on my bucket list is winning this grand final," she said.

"I have a t-shirt that says 'Just once before I die' with a Docker holding a question mark.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"My dream would be fulfilled. 32 years is a very, very long time.

"For all those years we've constantly been told what losers we are. We haven't won a cup; it's been a bit tough."

Ms Emmett, who dyed her hair purple after the Dockers stormed home against Sydney to seal their place in the grand final, will watch the game in the stands at the MCG.

She's flying via Sydney to avoid the skyrocketing airfares for direct flights from Perth to Melbourne.

Caroline Taylor and her daughter Junea tried for grand final tickets but missed out. (Aaron Bunch/AAP PHOTOS)

Junea Taylor, 17, put her name in the ballot for an MCG ticket but wasn't successful.

The high school student was only four years old the last time the Dockers played in a grand final.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"It would mean just so much. I've grown up as a fan my whole life, so seeing them win the flag, there will be tears," she said.

"This year is our year, and I reckon winning this year will give us the respect that Fremantle well and truly deserve."

Dockers fans were out in force at the team's training at Cockburn Oval. (Richard Wainwright/AAP PHOTOS)

She's heading to Fremantle, where tens of thousands of Dockers supporters are expected to watch the match in pubs and big screens in public areas.

The port city has become a sea of purple in recent weeks, with thousands of anchors adorning walls and lampposts.

There were jubilant scenes after Fremantle's gripping preliminary final win with fans flooding the city's cappuccino strip and some climbing onto the roofs of businesses.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Shop fronts proudly display "Go Dockers" and "Wharfie Time" posters, and restaurants are selling purple hamburgers and sausages.

WA Deputy Premier Rita Saffioti is hopeful of her team securing that elusive flag. (Aaron Bunch/AAP PHOTOS)

WA Deputy Premier and Treasurer Rita Saffioti and her family will be among the thousands of supporters heading east for the grand final.

"It would mean everything, to be honest," she said of an elusive Fremantle flag.

"Probably it would be one of the best experiences of my entire life.

"We've been through so many lows, and we haven't had the respect that we probably deserved."

title: Tradie's $36 Bunnings fix to crisis sweeping Aussie roads: 'Do it ourselves'
text:
A fed-up Australian tradie sick of the condition of the roads in his state has sought to fix the problem himself.

In Victoria, potholes have become a major headache for motorists — and a deadly hazard — with a recent Auditor-General's report finding the road network is deteriorating faster than it can be repaired.

In 2024, 48 per cent of state-managed roads were rated poor or very poor. That's up from 39 per cent in 2021.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

This year, criticism of the government's perceived inaction has ramped up, particularly ahead of the November election.

Melbourne-based tradie Nigel Carter was sick of waiting.

Last week, he decided to do something about it himself.

Nigel told Yahoo News Australia he's so far filled one hole and has plans to fill more.

Nigel and his companions can be seen in the video laying the bitumen and reversing over it with their car to set it in.

"We just went to Bunnings and bought some bitumen. We thought, since we pay a thousand bucks a year for rego and the potholes don't seem to get fixed, we thought we'd do it ourselves," he said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

At Bunnings, bitumen is priced at roughly $36 for 20 kilograms.

The group admitted the job might not have been perfect but said "at least we're helping."

"At least we did try to do something about it," he said.

Are potholes a problem near you? Contact

There's now one less pothole in Melbourne. Source: stigsxgarage

Victoria's pothole problems

While the video was a bit of a laugh, it points to a much darker problem in Victoria.

Earlier in September, a 71-year-old motorcyclist died following a crash on the Western Highway near Ballarat, after reportedly striking a pothole.

The issue has resulted in mounting pressure on the Victorian Government, with Nationals leader Danny O'Brien calling for urgent action and saying potholes "need to be fixed and fixed properly as a matter of urgency".

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

A recent RACV survey of more than 6,000 people found 71 per cent listed potholes and deteriorating road surfaces as their biggest road safety concern.

Monash University's Professor Jayantha Kodikara said, "Potholes are not simply a maintenance inconvenience".

"Once road deterioration reaches this stage, it can become a serious safety issue," he said.

"Potholes should be treated as a symptom, not a disease.

"If we focus only on filling the hole after it appears, we miss the opportunity to address the pavement design, moisture, construction quality and maintenance conditions that caused it."

Professor Kodikara said Australia has relied very successfully on thin-sealed unbound pavements for decades, but "traffic and climate conditions are changing".

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"We now need to reassess where these pavements remain the best solution and where stronger surfacing and pavement systems will deliver better whole-of-life value," he said.

The Victorian Government has announced $352 million for road maintenance, promising to double the number of potholes repaired this year from 250,000 to 500,000.

The Auditor-General, however, found the state faces a significant maintenance backlog.

It estimated more than $3 billion a year would be required to maintain road pavement conditions at their current level.
